question: Most common cause of secondary graft failure.
explanation: Despite being an "immunologically privileged" site, the most common cause of graft failure is irreversible, immunologic allograft rejection Reference: eyewiki

review.explanation: Primary graft failure is present from postoperative day 1 and reflects donor endothelial dysfunction; secondary (late) failure develops after an initially clear graft, and the leading cause is irreversible endothelial allograft rejection. The cornea is relatively immune privileged (avascular, no lymphatics, ACAID), but rejection still occurs in roughly 10-20 percent of low risk grafts and far more often in vascularized or inflamed host beds. Infection and glaucoma can each destroy a graft but account for far fewer failures, and glaucoma more often threatens the optic nerve than the endothelium.

question: Corneal degeneration with no other findings except for neovascularization.
explanation: Corneal degenerations typically feature the deposition of material, thinning of tissue, and neovascularization. Primary lipid keratopathy (LK) is infrequent and occurs spontaneously as stromal deposits of cholesterol and phospholipids. Primary LK is not associated with elevated serum lipids levels. The secondary form is associated with previous ocular injury or pathology. Unlike the primary form, secondary LK is far more common and is characteristically associated with corneal neovascularization (frequently one can find a characteristic dense yellow-white infiltrate associated with the presence of an adjacent corneal blood vessel) Reference: eyewiki

review.explanation: Lipid keratopathy is the degeneration defined by lipid (cholesterol and neutral fat) leaking out of corneal new vessels: a dense yellow-white stromal deposit sitting at the leading edge of a feeder vessel, in an otherwise normal cornea. Spheroidal (climatic droplet) degeneration produces golden oily droplets in the interpalpebral band from chronic UV exposure and is avascular; Coats white ring is a tiny iron residue ring at a healed metallic foreign body site; Salzmann nodules are elevated bluish-white subepithelial nodules following chronic keratitis, also avascular. Primary lipid keratopathy exists but is rare and occurs without vessels, so the vascularized secondary form is what this stem describes.

question: Corneal sensation
explanation: Innervation: Innervation to cornea occurs via CN V1 Approximately 70-80 branches of long posterior ciliary nerves enter peripheral cornea after myelin sheath is lost 1-2 mm before limbus: Reference: Fredman

review.explanation: Corneal sensation travels in the nasociliary branch of V1 by way of the long posterior ciliary nerves, which pierce the sclera near the optic nerve, run forward in the suprachoroidal space, and enter the peripheral cornea after losing their myelin sheaths 1-2 mm behind the limbus, which is how the most densely innervated tissue in the body stays transparent. The short posterior ciliary nerves accompany the short posterior ciliary arteries and are largely autonomic to the choroid, and there is no named sensory anterior ciliary nerve, only the anterior ciliary arteries travelling with the rectus muscles.

question: Which of the following medications is equal to 7 weeks of tetracycline in active trachoma treatment.
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document. Antibiotics of trachoma: A single dose of azithromycin (20 mg/kg up to 1 g) is the treatment of choice; Erythromycin 500 mg twice daily for 14 days or doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 10 days (tetracyclines are relatively contraindicated in pregnancy/breastfeeding and in children under 12).; Topical 1% tetracycline ointment is less effective than oral treatment 6 weeks after cataract extraction surgery (temporal incision), with a suture, the patient came to you with refraction of +1.00 -1.5 x180. The action to be considered is: Astigmatic keratotomy.; Removal the suture.; Bifocal.; IOL exchange.

review.explanation: A single oral dose of azithromycin (20 mg/kg, up to 1 g) is as effective as a prolonged course of topical tetracycline ointment, and it is the antibiotic arm of the WHO SAFE strategy precisely because directly observed single dosing solves the adherence problem that defeats weeks of topical therapy. Erythromycin is a fallback for patients who cannot take azithromycin but needs 500 mg twice daily for about two weeks, so it offers no single dose advantage and is not the intended answer.
review.concern: The stem says 7 weeks; the equivalence usually quoted in the trachoma literature is 6 weeks of topical tetracycline. A recall artifact that does not change the answer.

question: During phacoemulsification surgery, you suspected a posterior capsular tear. The best next step is:

options.A: Hold the foot pedal, and inject viscoelastic.
options.B: Take off the IA hand piece, and start vitrectomy.
options.C: Check the wound with weck cell

explanation: Management of Posterior Capsule Rent without Vitreous Loss The primary aim in such a case is to (a) Prevent enlargement of tear (b) Prevent vitreous prolapse into AC

review.explanation: The instant a posterior capsule tear is suspected, the priority is to prevent chamber shallowing, because a sudden pressure drop lets vitreous come forward and converts a small radial tear into a large one with lens material dropping posteriorly. So stop the foot pedal in position 0 with the instrument still in the eye, inject a dispersive viscoelastic through the side port to tamponade the vitreous face and hold the chamber, and only then withdraw the handpiece. Removing the handpiece first (B) is exactly the sequence that decompresses the eye; increasing infusion (D) hydrates the vitreous and enlarges the tear; the Weck-cell test (C) is an end-of-case check for vitreous at the wound, not the move for this moment.

question: During phacoemulsification surgery, the pupil failed to dilate. What is the best next step:

options.D: One drop of tropicamide 1% on the cornea.

explanation: A small pupil that is minimally responsive to dilating agents may be widened intraoperatively. The pupil can be bimanually stretched with Kuglen or Lester hooks, the iris can be tethered with hooks, or pupil-expansion devices can be employed. Viscodilation with a high-viscosity OVD is another method for pupil enlargement. AAO Further injection of the viscoelastic agent in the center of the miotic pupil causes the iris to stretch, deepening the anterior chamber and improving pupil dilation. This is also fairly effective in the absence of posterior synechiae. Alternatively, to dilate or maintain the dilated pupil, a pledget sponge soaked with dilating agents may be placed in the conjunctival sac for 10 to 20 minutes before surgery. Mydriatics such as epinephrine (0.3-0.5 ml of 1:1,000) may be added to the irrigation or the infusion bottle if an anterior chamber maintainer is placed. Otherwise, 0.5 to 1 ml sulfite and preservative-free epinephrine 1:1,000 diluted 1:3 in 1:3 xylocaine 4% and BSS-plus or 0.1 ml mixture of cyclopentholate 0.1%, phenylephrine 1.5% and xylocaine 1% may be injected into the anterior chamber before adding the viscoelastic agent. Epinephrine is especially effective in floppy iris syndrome. Surgical Management of Small Pupil Several mechanical maneuvers are available if the above fail.eyewiki Dispersive OVDs are materials that contain short-chain molecules that display low surface tension, which results in low molecular weight and low viscosity Reference: AAO, eyewiki

review.explanation: When the pupil will not dilate intraoperatively, mechanical expansion with iris retractor hooks or a Malyugin ring is the dependable answer, because it gives a stable controlled opening for the whole case and also tames a floppy iris. Viscomydriasis is a reasonable first move, but it is performed with a cohesive or viscoadaptive agent (Healon GV, Healon5) that pushes the iris peripherally, whereas a dispersive agent coats and stays put and is poor at stretching a pupil, so option B names the wrong OVD class. Intracameral lidocaine is an anaesthetic (it is intracameral phenylephrine or epinephrine that dilates), and topical tropicamide placed on the cornea mid surgery is washed away and far too slow to help.

question: One of the following viscoelastics is dispersive type:
explanation: Cohesive agents include Healon, Healon GV (Abbott Medical Optics, Santa Ana, CA); Amvisc, Amvisc Plus (Bausch + Lomb, Rochester, NY) and Provisc (Alcon, Ft Worth, TX). Dispersive agents include OcuCoat (Bausch + Lomb), Viscoat (Alcon), and Healon Endocoat (Abbott Medical Optics). Reference: eyewiki

review.explanation: Viscoat (chondroitin sulfate plus sodium hyaluronate) is the classic dispersive OVD: lower molecular weight and low pseudoplasticity, so it coats and clings to the endothelium and survives phaco turbulence. All three Healon products are cohesive, with Healon5 viscoadaptive: high molecular weight and high pseudoplasticity, so they aspirate out in a single bolus, which makes them excellent for maintaining space and easy to remove but poor endothelial protectants. The practical corollary is the soft-shell technique, dispersive against the endothelium and cohesive filling the centre.

question: Following cataract extraction surgery, the anterior capsule contracted and the IOL moved anteriorly. This will cause:
explanation: The anteriorly displaced lens has greater dioptric power and thus leads to a myopic shift Reference eyewiki

review.explanation: Effective lens position is one of the three variables in every IOL formula: for a given implanted power, moving the optic anteriorly increases its effective power in the eye and produces a myopic shift, roughly 1 D of refractive change per 0.5-1 mm of movement in an average eye and more with high power IOLs. Capsular contraction syndrome (anterior capsular phimosis) pulls the optic forward, so the eye becomes myopic; posterior displacement produces the opposite hyperopic shift. The same principle explains why a lens placed in the sulcus rather than the bag must be reduced by about 0.5-1.0 D.

question: Aniridia patient, developed glaucoma, and cataract which progressed and need extraction. What is most common intraoperative complication of cataract sx. for this patient:
explanation: Anterior or posterior polar lens opacities may be present at birth in patients with aniridia. Cortical, subcapsular, or lamellar opacities develop in 50%-85% of patients within the first 2 decades of life. The lens opacities may progress, further impairing vision. Poor zonular integrity and ectopia lentis have also been reported in patients with aniridia. Reference: AAO

review.explanation: Aniridia is a panocular PAX6 disorder, not just a missing iris: zonular weakness and frank ectopia lentis are well described, so zonular dialysis and capsular instability are the intraoperative problem, and many surgeons plan for a capsular tension ring and low-flow settings. Corneal problems in aniridia are real but they are limbal stem cell deficiency and aniridic keratopathy appearing over time, not an intraoperative event, and posterior capsule tears in these eyes are usually a downstream consequence of the zonular instability rather than the primary risk.

question: In phacoemulsification surgery, how to increase the flow rate : (may be not asking about the flow rate but the answer was C)

options.A: Change the pump from peristaltic to venturi.

explanation: The pump settings control the aspiration flow rate: The two main types of pumps in phaco systems are flow pumps (peristaltic) and vacuum pumps (venturi). Inflow rate: fluid inflow is based on gravity fluidics, and the infusion pressure is directly related to the bottle height. To create a pressure gradient the bottle is placed at a height above the patient. Reference eyewiki

review.explanation: Inflow in a conventional gravity-fed phaco machine is driven entirely by bottle or bag height above the eye, so raising the bottle raises infusion pressure and increases fluid flow through the anterior chamber, which is also how you keep the chamber stable when you push aspiration parameters up. The distractors test pump physiology: with a peristaltic (flow) pump the aspiration flow rate is set by pump speed in cc/min and is independent of the vacuum limit, whereas with a venturi (vacuum) pump flow is generated by the vacuum, so raising vacuum only raises flow on a venturi machine.
review.concern: The source itself flags this stem as an uncertain recall. If the examiner meant aspiration flow rate specifically on a peristaltic machine, the correct manipulation is the aspiration rate setting on the pump, not bottle height; bottle height governs inflow and infusion pressure.

question: The most common cause of inaccuracy in IOL calculation is:
explanation: From One Network (Axial length was not in the choices) Reference one network AAO, eyewiki

review.explanation: The three inputs to a theoretical IOL formula are axial length, keratometry and estimated lens position. Axial length error historically contributes the largest single share of postoperative refractive error, but it is not offered here, and keratometry is the next largest contributor and the one most easily corrupted in clinic by dry eye, contact lens warpage, prior refractive surgery or poor fixation. Option A is backwards: optical biometry is more accurate than contact applanation A-scan, which indents the cornea and falsely shortens the axial length.
review.concern: Axial length, the classic number one source of IOL calculation error, is absent from the option list (the source notes this too), so the question tests an incomplete list rather than the real hierarchy.

question: In IOL calculation, we make the target refraction slightly myopic because:

options.A: Error in calculation will not cause a hyperopic shift.
options.B: Slight myopia is more near to emmetropia.
options.C: Easy to deal with myopia rather than hyperopia

explanation: Most likely A some may benefit from either a hypermetropic or myopic status postoperatively. In cases where the patient prefers a certain refractive state for either occupational or social needs, including low vision aids Reference eyewiki, one network AAO

review.explanation: Aiming at a small myopic target, usually about -0.25 to -0.50 D, builds in a safety margin so that a refractive surprise still lands at or on the myopic side of plano rather than in hyperopia. That matters because a pseudophake has no accommodation: residual hyperopia leaves no clear focal distance at all and demands spectacles for everything, whereas the same magnitude of error toward myopia still leaves useful near or intermediate vision. Option B is simply false arithmetic, since slight myopia is no nearer emmetropia than slight hyperopia.
review.concern: Option C expresses essentially the same clinical idea as A in vaguer words, so the two are hard to separate as recalled; A is the better statement of the safety margin rationale.

question: A 35 year old patient with unilateral raise of IOP and iris defects. Most likely diagnosis is:
explanation: Reference: Kaniski

review.explanation: Unilateral disease plus secondary glaucoma plus iris changes (corectopia, iris atrophy, full thickness iris holes, ectropion uveae) in a young to middle aged adult, classically a woman in the third to fifth decade, is iridocorneal endothelial syndrome, in which abnormal proliferating ICE cells migrate across the angle and onto the iris and then contract. Axenfeld-Rieger is bilateral, congenital and autosomal dominant with posterior embryotoxon and dental and umbilical anomalies; acute angle closure gives a shallow chamber and a mid-dilated fixed pupil in a hyperopic eye, not focal iris holes. Specular microscopy showing the beaten bronze endothelium clinches it.

question: Post phacoemulsification surgery, a large decemet's detachment was detected. Your management is:
explanation: Most likely B It's the surgical reattachment of the detached DM with an injection of air and/or isoexpansile gases like perfluoropropane (C3F8, 12 - 14%) and sulfur hexafluoride (SF6, 15 - 20%). Gases reduce the need for reinjection due to their longer reabsorption time (SF6: 2 weeks and C3F8: 6 weeks). It has become the gold standard treatment for DMD management mainly due to its ease of execution and subsequent good outcomes. Small detachments may resolve spontaneously; other wise, the membrane may be reattached with air or an expansile gas (eg, sulfur hexafluoride [SF6 ] or perfluoropropane [C3 F8 ]) tamponade in the anterior chamber. Larger detachments can be sutured back into place under gas or an OVD. Reference: eyewiki, AAO, one network Treatment of Acanthameba involves all except:

review.explanation: A large Descemet membrane detachment will not settle spontaneously and is treated by descemetopexy, injecting a tamponading bubble into the anterior chamber to press the membrane back against the stroma. Non-expansile concentrations of isoexpansile gas (SF6 20 percent or C3F8 14 percent) are preferred over plain air for large detachments because they persist for weeks rather than a day or two and reduce the need for reinjection, and the chamber is deliberately only part filled to avoid pupillary block. Viscoelastic is the wrong choice altogether, since OVD left in the interface holds the membrane away from the stroma rather than reattaching it.
review.concern: Air descemetopexy is also an accepted standard treatment, and air is itself a gas, so options A and B overlap; the answer rests on the preference for longer acting gas in LARGE detachments.

question: Map-dot finger print dystrophy shows accumulation of:
explanation: In EBMD, extra sheets of basement membrane extend, abnormally, into the corneal epithelium (presenting as "maps"). Reference: eyewiki PED

review.explanation: Epithelial (anterior) basement membrane dystrophy, the map-dot-fingerprint pattern, is a disorder of abnormally thickened multilaminar epithelial basement membrane that grows up into the epithelium: the maps and fingerprint lines are redundant sheets and ridges of that basement membrane, and the dots are intraepithelial pseudocysts of trapped degenerating epithelial cells. Because hemidesmosomal attachment to the abnormal basement membrane is poor, the clinical consequence is recurrent corneal erosion and fluctuating irregular astigmatism. Bowman layer is the abnormal layer in Reis-Bucklers and Thiel-Behnke, not here.

question: All of the following mucopolysaccharidoses syndromes can cause RPE degeneration except: (From Kenneth Wright)
explanation: Ocular manifestations of Maroteaux-lamy: include corneal clouding, ptosis, acute and chronic angle-closure and open-angle glaucoma, optic nerve atrophy, and papilledema. Progressive corneal opacification affects all layers of the cornea and is one the primary contributors to low visual acuity in these patients. Retinal changes are not usually associated with MPS VI Reference: eyewiki

review.explanation: Retinal and RPE degeneration in the mucopolysaccharidoses tracks with heparan sulfate accumulation, so it is seen in MPS I (Hurler, Scheie, Hurler-Scheie), MPS II (Hunter) and MPS III (Sanfilippo). MPS VI (Maroteaux-Lamy) stores dermatan sulfate and produces dense progressive corneal clouding, glaucoma, optic neuropathy and papilloedema from raised intracranial pressure, but it characteristically spares the retina, as does MPS IV (Morquio). A useful cross-check for the same family of questions: Hunter is the X-linked one and the one classically said to lack corneal clouding, while Maroteaux-Lamy is the one that lacks retinopathy and preserves intellect.

question: In children, IOL calculation is challenging. The most likely cause is:

options.C: Increase of the diameter of the sulcus.
options.D: Increase diameter of capsulprehxis is not indicated in DR pt

explanation: The eye becomes slightly more hyperopic until 6-8 years of age, followed by a myopic shift toward emmetropia. Reference: AAO Botox mechanism of action:

review.explanation: A pseudophakic child's eye keeps growing, and normal axial elongation produces a progressive myopic shift that can exceed 5-6 D if the lens is implanted in infancy, so an IOL chosen for emmetropia today leaves a highly myopic teenager with a lens that cannot easily be changed. That is why the standard strategy is planned undercorrection, leaving the young child hyperopic by an amount scaled to age at surgery and managing the interim refractive error and amblyopia with spectacles or contact lenses. The eye does become slightly more hyperopic up to about 6-8 years before the myopic shift dominates, but it is the myopic shift over the lifetime of the implant that makes the calculation hard.
review.concern: Option D is garbled contaminated text carried over from a neighbouring question and is not a real distractor.

question: Brown syndrome. ONE FALSE:

options.A: Patients show down shoot on adduction.
options.C: Can be treated with recession of contralateral inferior rectus.
options.D: Associated with SO overreaction in the contralateral eye

explanation: Most likely D Mild congenital Brown syndrome does not require treatment, particularly because the condition may improve spontaneously over time, often after many years. Surgery is indicated for more severe congenital cases, for example, if a child with binocular visual potential is not achieving fusion or requires a large anomalous head posture for fusion. Superior oblique tenotomy nasal to the superior rectus muscle is effective; however, because it is likely to cause consecutive superior oblique muscle paresis, it is often combined with inferior oblique recession.AAO In this series, contralateral inferior rectus recession (5/15) or ipsilateral inferior oblique weakening procedure (8/15) were the most commonly performed secondary procedures. brown syndrome: surgical management. Several findings differentiate Brown syndrome from underelevation in adduction due to inferior oblique muscle paresis. Ipsilateral superior oblique overaction is typical of inferior oblique muscle paresis but is rare in Brown syndrome. AAO Reference: Understanding strabismus by Sameera, AAO, brown syndrome: surgical management.

referenceLinks.title: Brown Syndrome - EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Full article on Brown syndrome: limited elevation in adduction from superior oblique tendon-trochlea abnormality, congenital vs acquired forms, spontaneous resolution in 75-80% of asymptomatic cases, and surgical/steroid management

referenceLinks.title: Acute Acquired Brown Syndrome: 38-year-old Male with Ethmoidal Sinus Mucocele - EyeRounds (University of Iowa)
referenceLinks.shows: Figure 1 is a nine-cardinal-gaze clinical photo montage captioned 'note the under-elevation in adduction of the right eye' - exactly the figure this question needs; Figure 2 is the causative ethmoidal mass on MRI

figureFinding: Brown syndrome: limited elevation of the eye in adduction (superior oblique tendon-trochlea complex restriction), best shown on a nine-cardinal-gaze motility photo

review.explanation: Brown syndrome is a mechanical restriction of the superior oblique tendon-trochlea complex: the tendon cannot pay out, so the eye will not elevate in adduction, forced ductions are positive, there is often a downshoot in adduction with widening of the palpebral fissure in adduction, and a V pattern with divergence in upgaze. The single feature that separates it from an inferior oblique palsy is the ABSENCE of superior oblique overaction, since an IO palsy shows ipsilateral SO overaction with negative forced ductions, which makes statement D false, and doubly so for placing the overaction in the fellow eye. Mild congenital and acquired inflammatory cases genuinely can resolve spontaneously (B), and contralateral inferior rectus recession is a recognised secondary procedure for residual hypotropia in primary position (C).

question: Regarding strabismus surgery. ONE FALSE:

options.A: Jansen procedure for treatment of lateral rectus palsy.
options.B: Faden procedure with medial rectus recession for accommodative refractive esotropia.
options.C: Bimedial recti recession for infantile esotropia.
options.D: Bilateral recti resection for infantile esotropia.

explanation: When performing Jensen's procedure for lateral rectus palsy, limbal base incisions are made to expose the bellies of the lateral, superior and inferior rectus. Eyewiki In near esotropia: If the AC/A ratio > 8:1, then surgery is indicated in the form of recession of both the medial recti or a Faden suture on the recessed MR. Understanding strabismus by Sameera The most commonly performed initial procedure is recession of both medial rectus muscles. Recession of a medial rectus muscle combined with resection of the ipsilateral lateral rectus muscle is also effective. AAO Reference: Understanding strabismus by Sameera, AAO, eyewiki Homocystinuria. ONE TRUE:

review.explanation: For infantile esotropia the standard operation is recession of both medial recti, weakening the overacting adductors, or a unilateral medial rectus recession with lateral rectus resection. Resecting both medial recti would tighten the very muscles driving the crossing and increase the esotropia, so D is the false statement. Jensen muscle-union transposition is a genuine option for lateral rectus palsy (A), and a posterior fixation (Faden) suture on the medial recti combined with recession is the classic operation for esotropia with a high AC/A ratio (B).
review.concern: As recalled, option B says accommodative REFRACTIVE esotropia; purely refractive accommodative esotropia is treated with full hyperopic correction and not surgery, so taken verbatim B is also false. The original almost certainly read non-refractive (high AC/A) accommodative esotropia. D remains the safer answer because bilateral medial rectus resection for esotropia is wrong in principle.

question: A 40 year old patient developed spontaneous lens sublaxation (superior). Your diagnosis is:
explanation: Most likely B Trauma is the most common cause of acquired lens displacement. Nontraumatic ectopia lentis is commonly associated with Marfan syndrome, homocystinuria, aniridia, and congenital glaucoma. Ectopia lentis in Marfan syndrome is probably congenital in most cases. Progression of lens subluxation occurs in some patients over time, but in many patients the lens position remains stable homocystinuria: Subluxation typically begins between the ages of 3 and 10 years Reference: AAO

review.explanation: Non-traumatic ectopia lentis has a direction that gives the diagnosis away: Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1) subluxates the lens superotemporally with zonules stretched but usually intact, homocystinuria subluxates it inferonasally with disintegrated zonules and presents between about ages 3 and 10, and Weill-Marchesani produces a small spherical lens that moves anteriorly and causes pupillary block glaucoma. Trauma is the commonest cause of ectopia lentis overall, but the stem specifies spontaneous displacement, and traumatic subluxation moves away from the site of zonular rupture rather than reliably superiorly. Marfan lens dislocation is often congenital but can progress in adult life, which fits a 40 year old.

question: Patient with ET since birth, in which bimedial recti recession was done for about 6 years. He came to you complaining of intermittent upward movement of the left eye for most of the day. Your diagnosis:
explanation: Dissociated vertical deviation usually presents by age 2 years, whether or not any underlying horizontal strabismus has been surgically corrected. Either eye slowly drifts upward and outward, with simultaneous extorsion, when occluded or during periods of visual inattention. Reference: AAO, slef- assessment

review.explanation: Dissociated vertical deviation is a slow spontaneous upward drift, with extorsion and often abduction, of whichever eye is occluded or visually inattentive; it is bilateral though usually asymmetric, and crucially it violates Hering's law, so the fellow eye does not move downward as the drifting eye returns. It is tightly associated with infantile esotropia and typically appears around age 2 whether or not the horizontal deviation has been surgically corrected, exactly the history described. A consecutive hypertropia from surgery would be a constant vertical deviation measurable on cover testing, not an intermittent drift that comes and goes through the day.

question: Patient with history of infantile ET (OD). If you put a red lens in front of the left eye. ONE TRUE:

options.A: He will see a red light to the right of the white light.
options.B: He will see a red light to the left of the white light.

explanation: An esotropic patient will report the red circle to their right, which is uncrossed diplopia. Reference: Eyewiki

review.explanation: An esodeviation produces uncrossed (homonymous) diplopia: the esotropic right eye is turned nasally, so the straight-ahead target lands on its nasal retina and is projected temporally, that is, to the patient's right. The red filter here sits over the LEFT eye, which is the fixing eye, so the left eye's red image is in the true straight-ahead position while the right eye's white image is displaced to the right; the red therefore lies to the LEFT of the white. The trap is memorising 'esotropia equals red to the right', which is only correct when the filter is over the deviating right eye, so always reason from which eye is deviated and which carries the glass.
review.concern: The source's pasted explanation describes the standard right-eye-filter configuration, which reads as contradicting its own answer, but answer B is correct for the setup described. In practice a longstanding infantile esotrope suppresses and would report no diplopia at all.

question: Quantitative evaluation of strabismus. ONE FALSE:

options.A: Simultaneous prism cover test is used to measure tropia only.
options.B: Alternate cover-uncover test detects both tropia and phoria.
options.C: Monocular cover-uncover test doesn't differentiate tropia from phoria.

explanation: The simultaneous prism and cover test measures the manifest deviation during binocular viewing (only the heterotropia). The alternate cover test detects both latent and manifest deviations (ie, both heterophorias and heterotropias). The monocular cover-uncover test is the most important test for detecting manifest strabismus and for distinguishing a heterophoria (latent deviation) from a heterotropia (manifest deviation) Reference: AAO NURO

review.explanation: The monocular cover-uncover test is precisely the test that separates a phoria from a tropia, so statement C is false. Cover one eye and watch the OTHER: refixation movement means a manifest tropia. Then uncover and watch the eye that was covered: a recovery movement means a latent phoria that was broken by the cover. The simultaneous prism and cover test keeps both eyes viewing so it measures only the manifest deviation (A true), while the alternate cover test never allows fusion to be regained and therefore measures the total deviation, phoria plus tropia (B true).

question: Downbeat nystagmus is caused by all except:
explanation: Reference: AAO, eyewiki

referenceLinks.title: Nystagmus - EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Dedicated downbeat nystagmus section listing the exact etiologies in this question - structural lesions at the cervico-medullary junction, Arnold-Chiari type I, lithium and anticonvulsant toxicity, spinocerebellar degeneration, and nutritional causes (Wernicke encephalopathy, magnesium deficiency)

referenceLinks.title: Nystagmus Types - StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf)
referenceLinks.shows: Downbeat nystagmus defined as a vertical jerk oscillation signalling medullary-cervicomedullary junction lesions, intensifying on downgaze; lists Chiari I, cerebellar degenerations, magnesium depletion, and contrasts with peripheral vestibular nystagmus

figureFinding: Downbeat nystagmus - upward slow drift with corrective downward saccade, localizing to the cervicomedullary junction / vestibulocerebellum (flocculus); causes include Chiari I, spinocerebellar degeneration, lithium, alcohol/Wernicke

review.explanation: Downbeat nystagmus localises to the craniocervical junction and the cerebellar flocculus, with Chiari malformation the single most cited structural cause, and it is also produced by cerebellar and spinocerebellar degenerations and by toxic-metabolic insults including lithium, anticonvulsants, alcohol, and magnesium or thiamine deficiency. Middle ear and labyrinthine disease produce a peripheral vestibular nystagmus that is horizontal-torsional, suppresses with fixation and fatigues; a peripheral lesion essentially never produces a pure downbeat waveform. The practical rule is that any newly discovered downbeat nystagmus without a drug explanation earns MRI of the craniocervical junction.

question: Patient with left homonymous hemianopia. The MRI machine is not working and the CT scan is broken. How to isolate the lesion?
explanation: As noted previously, the OKN drum subtends a small portion of the visual field and therefore primarily tests smooth-pursuit movements in the direction of drum rotation and saccadic eye movements opposite the direction of drum rotation (eg, drum rotation toward the patient's left side generates a leftward ocular pursuit movement followed by a rightward saccade) patient with a hemous hemianopia due to a parietal lobe lesion will have a reduced OKN response with the target moving toward the affected side, whereas a patient with a homonymous hemianopia due to a lesion of the optic tract or occipital lobe will have an intact OKN response. Reference: AAO

review.explanation: With imaging unavailable, optokinetic testing is the bedside manoeuvre that separates a parietal from an occipital or optic tract cause of a homonymous hemianopia. Because the OKN drum subtends a small central field, it mainly tests smooth pursuit toward the direction of drum rotation with a corrective saccade the other way: the response is asymmetric and reduced when the target moves toward the side of the lesion in parietal lobe disease (Cogan's rule), and is intact with occipital or optic tract lesions.
review.concern: Pupil examination is an equally legitimate localiser here and might have been the intended answer: an optic tract lesion classically causes a contralateral relative afferent pupillary defect (in this case the left eye) plus band or bow-tie optic atrophy. The question as recalled has two defensible answers, so do not treat D as the only correct localising test.

question: Patient with isolated 6th nerve palsy. The least important exam:
explanation: Adults: - Check blood pressure, fasting blood sugar, and hemoglobin A1c. - MRI of the brain is indicated for the following patients: Younger than 45 years of age (if MRI is negative, consider LP), Patients aged 45 to 55 years with no vasculopathic risk factors, Sixth cranial nerve palsy accompanied by severe pain or any other neurologic or neuro-ophthalmic signs, Any history of cancer, Bilateral sixth cranial nerve palsies, Papilledema is present. - Immediate ESR, CRP, and platelet count if GCA is suspected. - Consider Lyme antibody. Children - Otoscopic examination to rule out complicated otitis media. - MRI of the brain in all children. Well's Reference: Well's

review.explanation: An isolated sixth nerve palsy in an adult is usually microvascular, so the workup is blood pressure, glucose and HbA1c, plus immediate ESR, CRP and platelets if giant cell arteritis is plausible, with MRI reserved for patients under about 45-50, bilateral or progressive palsies, associated neurological or neuro-ophthalmic signs, severe pain, papilloedema or a cancer history (and MRI for every child). Catheter angiography exists to hunt aneurysms, which is the concern in a pupil-involving THIRD nerve palsy, not a sixth, so it is both the least informative and the most invasive test on this list.

question: Regarding VEP. ONE FALSE:

options.A: It is an essential test for optic nerve.
options.B: Latency increased in optic neuritis recovery.
options.C: Amplitude increase in optic neuritis recovey
options.D: Usually there is no abnormality in albinism.

explanation: Most likely D VEP depends on the integrity of the visual pathway including eye, optic nerve, optic chiasm, optic tract, optic radiation and cerebral cortex. Optic Optic neuritis In Acute stage: The VEP P100 amplitude is reduced or even not recordable. During the acute stage, the optic nerve fibres can become demyelinated, and thus, the VEP P100 latency is also prolonged. neuritis In recovery stage: By 4 to 7 weeks, the fields recovered to near normal sensitivity in most locations, and visual acuity returned to 20/20. The mVEP recovered to nearly full amplitude in all regions, but substantial delays were present in many locations. The delayed responses were associated with regions of visual field loss documented during the acute phase. Along with the visual acuity improvement, there is a recovery in the VEP P100 amplitude, while the VEP P100 latency continues to be prolonged due to demyelinated optic nerve fibres In remyelination stage: To follow possible remyelination. Within a month of the onset of symptoms, remyelination by oligodendrocytes starts at the edges of plaques. The subsequent shortening of the VEP latency represents a sign of remyelination of the optic nerve, which is not associated with visual acuity improvement [29]. Thus, the VEP latency can remain abnormal for many years, while there is a tendency for it to shorten over a period of 2 years or more.pubmed: jelka brecelj Albinism is associated with fiber over-decussation, resulting in crossing of up to 90% of fibers to the contralateral side and thus strabismus and loss of stereopsis. Evidence of this abnormality can be detected by 3-lead visual evoked potential (VEP) for proper counseling regarding visual potential of a patient. Eyewiki Asymmetric visually evoked potentials often are seen in albinism patients and may be helpful in diagnosis. AAO Reference: PubMed: jelka brecelj, AAO, eyewiki

review.explanation: The VEP is one of the few objective tests of the whole postretinal pathway, and it is a diagnostic test IN albinism: excessive decussation of temporal retinal fibres at the chiasm produces the characteristic crossed asymmetry of the response recorded over the two hemispheres, so saying albinism is usually normal on VEP is false. In optic neuritis the P100 amplitude collapses acutely and then recovers as acuity returns, but the P100 latency stays prolonged more or less permanently because remyelination is incomplete, which is why statements B and C are both true and why a delayed but normal-amplitude P100 is the signature of an old demyelinating attack.

Choroidal effusion accompanies hypotony and shares the same picture, and both reverse when the pressure is restored. review.explanation: Diabetic retinopathy is the classic pregnancy progressor, worse with poor pre-pregnancy control, longer duration of diabetes, coexisting hypertension and abrupt tightening of glycaemia. Meningiomas enlarge in pregnancy because they carry progesterone receptors and because of the increase in plasma volume, and keratoconus progression with corneal steepening in pregnancy is described and attributed to hormonal effects on corneal biomechanics. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is the outlier: its incidence in pregnancy matches that of non-pregnant women of the same age and weight, pregnancy does not alter its course or outcome, and it is not an indication for termination or for caesarean delivery.

question: Which one is true regarding muscle of riolan
explanation: The muscle of Riolan, lies more posterior than the main portion of the orbicularis and creates the gray line. The muscle of Riolan may play a role in meibomian glandular discharge, blinking, and eyelash position. Reference: AAO

review.explanation: The muscle of Riolan is the fine pretarsal marginal slip of orbicularis that runs just behind the lash follicles and forms the grey line, the surgical landmark that separates anterior from posterior lamella and the plane used when splitting the lid. Its accepted functions are keeping the eyelid margin and puncta apposed to the globe, helping express meibomian secretion into the tear film, and stabilising the blink; loss of that apposition contributes to epiphora and margin instability.
review.concern: Standard texts (including the AAO passage the source quotes) also credit the muscle of Riolan with influencing eyelash position, which makes option A partly defensible. The recall offers only two coarse alternatives, so the discrimination is soft.

question: Necrotizing vasculitis is caused by all except:
explanation: most likely D Necrotizing vasculitis may be the primary condition such as polyarteritis nodosa or granulomatosis with ANCA associated vasculitis (formerly called Wegener granulomatosis). In other cases, the vasculitis may occur as part of another disorder, such as systemic lupus erythematosus or hepatitis C. Takayasu's arteritis (TA) is a large-vessel vasculitis pathologically characterized by granulomatous necrotizing vasculitis with giant cells. Reference: NIH, Pubmed (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5996549/)

review.explanation: A dissecting or ascending aortic aneurysm is a structural failure of the media (cystic medial degeneration, as in Marfan syndrome or long-standing hypertension), not an inflammatory destruction of the vessel wall, so it is not a vasculitis at all. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is the prototype necrotizing ANCA-associated vasculitis, systemic lupus produces an immune-complex necrotizing vasculitis, and Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel granulomatous arteritis with necrotizing features and giant cells. The ophthalmic relevance is that the genuine vasculitides on this list are exactly the diseases that cause necrotizing scleritis and peripheral ulcerative keratitis.

question: Regarding myasthenia gravis. ONE TRUE:

options.B: The majority of MG patients have ocular involvement.
options.C: Single fiber EMG will show decrease jitter.

explanation: An ice pack is applied to the affected upper eyelid for 2-5 minutes. A positive test is the improvement of ptosis by > 2mm or more In MG the most common presenting signs are ocular. Of these, the most common sign is ptosis. EMG in MG: ■ repetitive stimulation → decremental response ■ single fibre electromyography shows increased jitter (80-100% sensitivity) Reference: eyewiki, Toronto notes

review.explanation: Ocular involvement is the rule rather than the exception in myasthenia gravis: more than half of patients present with ptosis or diplopia and roughly 90 percent develop ocular signs at some point, which is why the ophthalmologist so often makes the diagnosis. Option A is inverted, since cooling the lid with an ice pack for 2 minutes improves neuromuscular transmission and lifts the ptosis by 2 mm or more, which is a POSITIVE test. Option C is also inverted: single fibre EMG shows INCREASED jitter (80-100 percent sensitivity) and repetitive stimulation shows a decremental response.

question: Patient with congenital membranous NLDO and stenosis of both upper and lower canaliculi. The best management is:
explanation: Reference: one network AAO

review.explanation: The obstruction here sits at two levels, a membranous block at the valve of Hasner plus stenosis of BOTH canaliculi, and bicanalicular (Crawford) silicone intubation is the single option that stents the upper canaliculus, the lower canaliculus, the common canaliculus and the nasolacrimal duct together while the membranous obstruction is opened. Monocanalicular intubation would leave the second stenosed canaliculus untreated; a pigtail probe is reserved for repairing canalicular lacerations and risks injuring an intact common canaliculus; and DCR is not the primary operation for a congenital membranous obstruction, which usually responds to probing with intubation and is reserved for failures or for true bony/duct obstruction.
review.concern: The stem is a terse recall and gives no age or history of prior probing, both of which would ordinarily shape the choice.

question: Lefort II. ONE FALSE:

explanation: Zugoma is intact in Le Fort II Le Fort Type I (Horizontal) Le Fort Type I fracture is a horizontal fracture of the lower maxilla from the midface, without orbital involvement, causing a freely mobile tooth-baring upper jaw and hard palate. Le Fort Type II (Pyramidal) Le Fort Type II fracture is a pyramidal shaped fracture along the nasal bridge, involving the inferomedial orbital rim and orbital floor, and causes separation of the midface from the skull base. fractures along the nasal bridge, frontal maxilla, lacrimal bones, orbital floor and inferior rim near the inferior orbital foramen, through the anterior wall of the maxillary sinus, and through the pterygoid plates. Le Fort Type III (Transverse, aka Craniofacial Dysfunction) Le Fort III fracture, also called a craniofacial dysfunction, is a transverse fracture that creates posterior orbital fractures to separate the entire midface from the skull base, sparing the optic canal. This occurs from force delivered at the orbital level and nasal bridge (upper maxilla) causing fractures along the medial orbital wall, through the nasolacrimal groove and ethmoid bones, along the orbital floor and inferior orbital fissure, along the lateral orbital wall, through zygomatic arch, ethmoid, and pterygoid processes. review.explanation: Le Fort II is the pyramidal fracture: it runs across the nasal bridge, down through the frontal process of the maxilla and the lacrimal bone, across the medial orbital wall and the orbital floor near the infraorbital foramen, then through the anterior wall of the maxillary sinus and back to the pterygoid plates, freeing a pyramid of central midface from the skull base. The zygomatic arch and the lateral orbital rim remain intact in Le Fort II; arch and zygomaticofrontal suture involvement with complete craniofacial disjunction defines Le Fort III. Le Fort I is the low transverse fracture that floats the palate and upper teeth with no orbital involvement at all.

question: Regarding orbital decompression. ONE FALSE:

options.A: Lateral wall decompression gives the maximum decrease of proptosis.
options.B: Inferior wall decompression may worsen the diplopia.
options.C: Medial wall decompression can be done transconjuctival or trans-sphenoidal.

explanation: most likely A Patients with more enlargement of the orbital fat compartment (type I orbitopathy) may benefit from more fatty decompression, whereas patients with more extraocular muscle enlargement (type II orbitopathy) may benefit from more bony decompression. Most surgery is undertaken via an external approach, though the medial wall and the medial part of the floor can be reached endoscopically. One-wall (deep lateral) decompression is effective (approximately 4-5 mm reduction in proptosis) and may reduce the risk of postoperative diplopia; two-wall (balanced medial and lateral) decompression provides a greater effect but with a significant risk of inducing diplopia; three-wall decompression includes the floor with a reduction in proptosis of 6-10 mm but may lead to hypoglobus and carries a higher risk of infraorbital nerve damage and diplopia; very severe proptosis may require removal of part of the orbital roof in addition (four-wall decompression). (Kaniski) This approach reduces proptosis by 2-4 mm. This socalled "balanced - medial and lateral wall" two-wall decompression is not associated with the high rates of postoperative diplopia that often resulted after decompression by removal of the orbital floor and medial wall.(Nerad) Decompression of the lateral wall can be achieved by using rongeurs and/or a drill to remove bone along the sphenoid wing. A retrocaruncular incision allows an excellent approach to the medial orbital wall; it can be used in conjunction with a transconjunctival incision for further access. Alternatively, a transnasal endoscopic approach to the medial orbit via the ethmoid sinus may be used to access the medial wall. AAO Reference: Nerad, Kanaski, AAO, eyewiki

review.explanation: Proptosis reduction in thyroid eye disease scales with how many walls are removed: a single deep lateral wall gives roughly 4-5 mm, a balanced two-wall (medial plus lateral) decompression gives more, and a three-wall decompression including the floor gives about 6-10 mm, so calling the lateral wall alone the maximum is the false statement. The floor and the posteromedial strut are exactly where new or worsened diplopia comes from as the globe drops and rotates, which makes B true, and the medial wall genuinely can be reached transcaruncular or transconjunctivally from the orbit or endonasally through the ethmoids, which makes C true as loosely worded.
review.concern: The deep lateral wall approach is popular precisely because it gives good decompression with LESS induced diplopia, so statement A fails only on the strict claim of 'maximum' reduction. If the recalled wording differed, this discrimination could change.

question: Regarding Kaposi sarcoma. ONE FALSE:

options.A: It is not responsive to radiotherapy.
options.B: Seen in lower limb among immunocompromised pt.

explanation: frequent manifestation of AIDS, although it may also occur in elderly or immunocompromised patients, such as those who have received organ transplants. Conjunctival lesions can be mistaken for a foreign-body granuloma or cavernous hemangioma. The lesion is composed of spindle cells of probable endothelial origin. It may be treated with cryotherapy, excision, radiation, or intralesional chemotherapeutic agents. If Kaposi sarcoma is related to AIDS, it may regress with adequate antiviral treatment of the underlying HIV infection Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) typically presents as multiple bilateral cutaneous patches or plaques of the lower extremities. Reference: AAO, Pubmed

review.explanation: Kaposi sarcoma is notably radiosensitive, and low-dose radiotherapy is a standard local treatment for conjunctival and eyelid lesions alongside excision, cryotherapy and intralesional chemotherapy, so 'not responsive to radiotherapy' is the false statement. It is an HHV-8 driven spindle cell vascular tumour of probable endothelial origin, appearing classically as multiple violaceous cutaneous plaques on the lower limbs in the elderly Mediterranean form and disseminated in AIDS and transplant patients. A bright red subconjunctival Kaposi lesion is regularly mistaken for a subconjunctival haemorrhage or a foreign body granuloma, and in HIV-associated disease effective antiretroviral therapy alone often produces regression.

question: Regarding necrotizing fasciitis. ONE FALSE:

options.A: Can be treated by intravenous peniciline (mega dose)
options.B: debridement should be done in the first 24 hours.
options.C: Skin might show no abnormalities in early phase, even in severe infection

explanation: ? (Penicillin is used with other drugs and in case gram +ve result) The mainstay of treatment for NF is surgical intervention with serial debridement coupled with aggressive antibiotic therapy, fluid resuscitation, and blood pressure support. Early recognition and initiation of treatment help to decrease morbidity and mortality. There are only a handful of cases of periorbital NF that have successfully been treated with medical intervention alone. Antimicrobial coverage includes aerobes (including MRSA), and anaerobes. Combinations may include vancomycin plus one of the following (1) piperacillin- tazobactam, (2) a carbapenem, (3) ceftriaxone plus metronidazole, (4) fluoroquinolone metronidazole. Clindamycin should be added as it suppresses streptococcal toxin and cytokine production. Eyewiki Necrotizing soft tissue infection is a surgical emergency. Radiographic imaging studies should not delay surgical intervention when there is crepitus on examination or rapid progression of clinical manifestations. UTD The initial clinical presentation is similar to that of orbital or preseptal cellulitis, with swelling, erythema, and pain, but it may be accompanied by a shocklike syndrome. Because necrotizing fasciitis tends to track along avascular tissue planes, an early sign may be anesthesia over the affected area caused by involvement of deep cutaneous nerves. In addition, reports of disproportionate pain may suggest the presence of necrotizing fasciitis, as do skin color changes that progress from rose to bluegray, with bullae formation and frank cutaneous necrosis. AAO Acceptable empiric antibiotic regimens include: ●A carbapenem or beta-lactam-beta- lactamase inhibitor plus ●An agent with activity against methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA; such as vancomycin or linezolid) (table 3). In neonates and children, vancomycin (15 mg/kg/dose every six to eight hours) is the usual empiric antibiotic for MRSA; the six- hour dosing interval is employed for sicker children plus ●Clindamycin, for its antitoxin effects against toxin-elaborating strains of streptococci and staphylococci (600 to 900 mg intravenously [IV] every eight hours in adults; 40 mg/kg per day divided every eight hours in children and neonates). UTD Reference: eyewiki, UTD, AAO

review.explanation: Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency: the mainstay is urgent and repeated debridement of all necrotic fascia, with antibiotics, fluid resuscitation and haemodynamic support as adjuncts, so presenting high dose intravenous penicillin as the treatment is the false statement. Empiric cover must be broad (typically vancomycin plus a beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor or a carbapenem) with clindamycin added to switch off streptococcal exotoxin and cytokine production, narrowing to penicillin plus clindamycin only once group A Streptococcus is confirmed. Statement C is the key clinical pearl: early on the overlying skin can look almost normal while the patient has pain grossly out of proportion, and delaying surgery to obtain imaging costs lives.
review.concern: High dose penicillin with clindamycin genuinely is the definitive antibiotic regimen for streptococcal necrotizing fasciitis, so A is false only because it implies medical therapy in place of surgery. It is the answer by elimination, since B and C are unambiguously true.

question: Patient with treated HZV keratopathy, came to you with history of lagophthalmus for 3 months. The management now is:
explanation: most likely B Neurotrophic ulcers of herpes zoster are best treated by tarsorrhaphy of the lateral half of the lids. Reference: Parson's

review.explanation: Post-herpetic neurotrophic keratopathy is the collision of a cornea that cannot feel with a lid that cannot close, and three months of persistent lagophthalmos is not a problem that drops will solve. Lateral tarsorrhaphy shortens the palpebral fissure, protects the exposed cornea and restores an effective tear film, and it is the classic answer for neurotrophic and exposure ulceration after herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Antiviral therapy addresses active viral replication and does nothing for an anaesthetic, mechanically exposed cornea, which is why acyclovir is the wrong reflex here.
review.concern: A stepwise approach would begin with intensive preservative-free lubrication and ointment at night, and the stem does not state what has already been tried; at three months, however, a lid procedure is the definitive answer.

Medial canthal defects are handled by direct closure when small, by a glabellar or median forehead flap for larger ones, by full thickness skin grafting, or by leaving the concavity to granulate (laissez-faire), which heals unusually well in this location.

question: In Lateral tarsal strip, you will make the lateral canthus:
explanation: Remember also to place the lateral canthal tendon slightly higher than the medial canthal tendon to recreate the normal slight upward slant to the lateral canthus. Reference: Nerad The correct order of TED surgeries is:

review.explanation: The normal canthal tilt is upward, with the lateral canthal angle sitting roughly 1-2 mm HIGHER than the medial canthus, so the tarsal strip is fixated to reproduce that slight upward slant; setting it level or low produces a rounded, downturned, aged-looking canthus and often leaves residual laxity. The strip must be sutured to periosteum on the INNER aspect of the lateral orbital rim at Whitnall's (lateral orbital) tubercle, about 2-3 mm inside the rim, so the lid hugs the globe, which is why option D (outside the rim) is wrong. Lockwood's ligament is the inferior suspensory hammock of the globe, not a canthal insertion.

question: All of the following can cause hearing loss except: (From Friedman)
explanation: Usher's syndrome (AR): most common syndrome associated with RP; mapped to chromosome 1q41 (USH2A) Findings: RP and deafness; ataxia, MR, low phosphate (rickets), muscle wasting 10-20% of RP patients are deaf; 5% of congenitally deaf individuals have Usher's type I Alstrom's disease: mapped to chromosome 2p13 (ALMS1) RP with profound visual loss in 1st decade of life; diabetes, obesity, deafness, renal failure, baldness, acanthosis nigricans, hypogenitalism Cockayne's syndrome: RP with profound visual loss by 2nd decade of life; dwarfism, deafness, mental retardation, premature aging, psychosis, intracranial calcifications Refsum's disease (AR): deficiency of phytanic acid oxidase interferes with fatty acid metabolism Findings: atypical RP (often sine pigmento or starts in macula), cataracts, prominent corneal nerves Other findings: ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, deafness, anosmia, ichthyosis, cardiac abnormalities, hypotonia, hepatomegaly, mental retardation. Reference: Fredman A possible cause of peripheral neovascularization:

review.explanation: All four of these retinal dystrophy syndromes are described with sensorineural hearing loss, and the only defensible discriminator is how central deafness is to each definition. Usher syndrome is defined by retinitis pigmentosa plus congenital deafness, Alstrom syndrome by cone-rod dystrophy with obesity, insulin resistance, cardiomyopathy and deafness, and Cockayne syndrome by dwarfism, premature ageing, intracranial calcification, retinal degeneration and deafness. Refsum disease is defined by its tetrad of atypical retinitis pigmentosa, peripheral polyneuropathy, cerebellar ataxia and raised CSF protein from phytanic acid accumulation, with deafness, anosmia, ichthyosis and cardiac conduction defects as associated rather than defining features.
review.concern: This question is not sound as recalled: sensorineural hearing loss IS a recognised feature of Refsum disease, and the source's own explanation lists deafness under Refsum while answering C. Either an option was mis-recalled (the classic RP syndromes WITHOUT deafness are Bardet-Biedl and Bassen-Kornzweig/abetalipoproteinaemia) or the examiner wanted the Refsum tetrad. Low confidence; do not memorise 'Refsum has no deafness'.

question: According to the ETDRS. ONE TRUE:

options.A: Aspirin found to decrease morbidity of DR.
options.B: PRP should be done for patients with any neovascularization of the disc.
options.C: PRP should be done for patients with Type2 DM and severe NPDR.

explanation: Most likely C Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study: Conclusions: treat all patients with CSME regardless of vision Immediate PRP should be reserved for patients with high-risk PDR and possibly those with severe NPDR in both eyes No benefit from aspirin (650 mg/day). Reference: Fredman

review.explanation: ETDRS concluded that scatter photocoagulation should be DEFERRED in mild to moderate NPDR but considered as eyes approach high-risk PDR, and the subgroup that benefited most from early scatter treatment was type 2 diabetics with severe or very severe NPDR or early PDR, which is exactly statement C. Aspirin 650 mg/day neither slowed retinopathy progression nor increased vitreous haemorrhage, so A is false; the real message of the aspirin arm was that aspirin is SAFE in diabetic retinopathy. B overtreats: PRP is indicated for HIGH-RISK PDR, meaning NVD greater than about one third of a disc area, or any NVD or NVE of at least half a disc area accompanied by vitreous or preretinal haemorrhage, not for any disc neovascularisation at all.

question: Aflipecept (Eylea) is a new Anti-VEGF, FDA approved on 2012 for treatment of AMD. It is:
explanation: Aflibercept is a recombinant fusion protein consisting of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-binding portions from the extracellular domains of human VEGF receptors 1 and 2, that are fused to the Fc portion of the human IgG1 immunoglobulin. Reference: FDA

review.explanation: Aflibercept is a soluble decoy receptor: the VEGF-binding domains of VEGF receptors 1 and 2 fused to the Fc portion of human IgG1, which is why it is called a fusion protein (and was developed as VEGF Trap-Eye). That construction gives much higher binding affinity than the antibody-based agents and lets it also bind VEGF-B and placental growth factor. Learn the class of each drug together: pegaptanib is the aptamer, bevacizumab the full-length humanised monoclonal antibody, ranibizumab the antibody fragment (Fab), and aflibercept and conbercept the fusion proteins.

explanation: The source is undecided between B and C. both are ture >70% bilateral, but asymmetric. Eyewiki They may be isolated or dominantly inherited. AAO Autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance is suspected. Eyewiki Deep or buried drusen tend not to demonstrate NFL thinning; however, calcification can be detected with B-scan ultrasound or computed tomography. Unfortunately, ONHD enlarge with age, and both thinning of the NFL and field loss are slowly progressive over time. Eyewiki Optic nerve drusen or coloboma are other possible causes of glaucomatous-appearing visual field loss. AAO Reference: AAO, eyewiki

review.explanation: Optic disc drusen are calcified hyaline bodies within the prelaminar optic nerve head, and familial occurrence is well described with autosomal dominant inheritance of incomplete penetrance, which is why examining relatives of an affected patient is worthwhile. Option A is false, since drusen are bilateral in roughly 70-75 percent of cases though often strikingly asymmetric, and option D is false, since drusen do not cause glaucoma even though the nerve fibre layer loss they produce mimics glaucomatous field defects (enlarged blind spot, arcuate and nasal steps).
