options.C: -2ndry focal point is in front of retina
options.D: -axial myopia is associated with high corneal refractive power

explanation: Categorized: optical Axial Myopia: "a myopic refractive state that can be attributed to excessive axial elongation". Refractive Myopia: "a myopic refractive state that can be attributed to changes in the structure or location of the image forming structures of the eye, i.e. the cornea and/or lens".

review.explanation: Axial myopia is by definition a myopic refractive state attributable to excessive axial elongation with an otherwise ordinary cornea and lens, whereas myopia produced by an unusually steep, powerful cornea or an over-powered lens is refractive myopia; option D therefore contradicts the definition and is the exception. High myopia is conventionally defined as -6.00 D or greater, refractive lens exchange (clear lens extraction) is a recognised though not first-line option in high myopes who are unsuitable for corneal surgery or a phakic IOL, and by definition the myopic eye focuses parallel light in front of the retina.

question: Retained lens fiber nuclei in all except:
explanation: Categorized: AS

review.explanation: Retention of cell nuclei deep within the lens, where nuclei should have been lost during fibre maturation, is the classic histological signature of congenital rubella cataract and is also described in Lowe syndrome and in trisomy 13. Congenital syphilis damages the eye through interstitial keratitis, a salt-and-pepper chorioretinopathy, and occasionally optic atrophy or uveitis, but it is not associated with retained lens fibre nuclei, so it is the exception. A related pearl is that live rubella virus can persist inside the lens for years, which is why lens material should be handled carefully at surgery.

question: Most common cause of blindness worldwide:
explanation: Categorized: AS

review.explanation: Cataract remains the leading cause of blindness worldwide, accounting for roughly a third to a half of cases in global surveys, and it is the leading avoidable cause because the treatment is a single effective operation. Diabetic retinopathy is a major cause of blindness in working-age adults in high-income countries but contributes a much smaller share globally. Uncorrected refractive error is the leading cause of visual impairment overall and of presenting visual impairment, but it causes relatively little blindness as strictly defined.
review.concern: The answer depends on the endpoint: cataract leads for blindness, whereas uncorrected refractive error leads for moderate to severe visual impairment. The stem says blindness, so cataract is right, but examiners do sometimes phrase this loosely.

question: In regards to tonometry , all true except

options.A: -it'll be artificially high post PRK and lasik
options.C: -Scleral buckle will give artificially low reading

explanation: Categorized: Glaucoma Numerous studies have documented a change in measured intraocular pressure (IOP) after LASIK, PRK, and other refractive surgeries. While the procedures themselves may cause a change in intraocular pressure, as with Steroid Glaucoma after LASIK or interface fluid[1], in most cases the true IOP remains the same and only the measurement is affected. The change in corneal biomechanics after refractive surgery causes a false underestimation of IOP that is more pronounced with applanation and indentation tonometry. Since a falsely low IOP reading may lead to a delay in diagnosis of ocular hypertension or glaucoma, ophthalmologists should be aware of the difficulty in obtaining true IOP readings after refractive surgery. Reference: https://eyewiki.aao.org/Tonometry_after_Refractive_Surgery Man wearing right plano lens and left -10 lens , has xt of 40 prisms , if you ask patient to look to distance fixing with right eye his xt will be: 20; 30; 40; 50 Categorized:Ped

review.explanation: After LASIK or PRK the cornea is thinner and biomechanically weaker, so Goldmann applanation systematically underestimates the true IOP; the statement that readings will be artificially high is therefore the false one. This matters clinically because a falsely reassuring pressure can mask a post-LASIK steroid response or interface fluid syndrome and delay the diagnosis of glaucoma. Intrastromal ring segments thicken and stiffen the cornea and tend to give falsely high readings, a scleral buckle is quoted as giving falsely low readings, and an excess of fluorescein widens the mires so that the endpoint is reached prematurely and the pressure is overestimated.

question: Patient came to you with XT 30 distance, 10 near , after +3 D lens placed for 30 minutes, his angle was 30 distance 25 near? This patient has
explanation: Categorized: PED Reference: self assessment

review.explanation: This is the standard manoeuvre for unmasking a high AC/A ratio. In true divergence excess the distance deviation still exceeds the near deviation by 10 to 15 prism dioptres or more even after accommodative and proximal convergence have been eliminated, whereas in simulated (pseudo) divergence excess the near angle climbs to within about 10 prism dioptres of the distance angle once accommodative convergence is blocked. Here +3.00 D lenses at near raised the near deviation from 10 to 25 against a distance angle of 30, so the true near angle is close to the distance angle and this is pseudo-divergence excess. Basic exotropia has near and distance angles within 10 prism dioptres from the outset, and convergence insufficiency shows the near angle much larger than the distance angle.

review.explanation: Magnification in indirect ophthalmoscopy is inversely related to the power of the condensing lens, so a 15 D lens gives a larger but narrower view than a 20 D lens and a 28 D lens gives a wide but small image; that trade-off between field and magnification is the governing principle. In practice the examiner also enlarges the view by withdrawing the condensing lens slightly from the patient's eye, which narrows the bundle accepted, reduces the field and brings the aerial image nearer the observer, and this appears to be what the key describes. The eyepieces of a binocular indirect cannot be removed without abolishing stereopsis, and simply approaching the patient's own lens does not change the size of the aerial image the condensing lens forms.

The physically dependable answers to this question are to use a lower-power condensing lens or to bring the observer closer to the aerial image; treat the item as unreliable as written.

question: +2.00 -4.00 *90 what the type of astigmatism:
explanation: Categorized: optical

review.explanation: Rewrite the prescription in terms of its two principal meridians: +2.00 -4.00 x 90 gives +2.00 D in the 90 degree meridian and +2.00 minus 4.00, that is -2.00 D, in the 180 degree meridian. One focal line therefore lies behind the retina and the other in front of it, which is by definition mixed astigmatism. Simple hyperopic or simple myopic astigmatism requires one meridian to be emmetropic (plano), and compound myopic astigmatism requires both meridians to be myopic, neither of which applies here.

question: Basal Cell carcinoma which is true?

options.A: Show retained polarity with peripheral nuclear palisading

explanation: Categorized: Oclo or pathology

review.explanation: Basal cell carcinoma consists of nests of basaloid cells that show peripheral palisading of nuclei with retraction artefact from the surrounding stroma, and this orderly peripheral arrangement is the classic histological description, so option A is correct. It is the commonest eyelid malignancy and clearly favours the lower lid and medial canthus, the areas of greatest cumulative sun exposure, so the claim that it is commoner on the upper lid is false. The tumour with an upper lid predilection is sebaceous carcinoma, because the upper tarsus contains more meibomian glands, and that is the great masquerader to keep in mind for recurrent unilateral blepharoconjunctivitis.

question: AMD risk factor?
explanation: Categorized: Retina Risk Factors Age ARMD risk increases with age. The risk increases more than three-fold in patients older than 75 years of age compared to the group of patients between 65-74 years of age (Beaver Dam Eye Study; Framingham Eye Study).[3][8] Cigarette Smoking A ten pack-year tobacco smoking history is associated with increased development of exudative age-related macular degeneration.[9][10] After controlling for confounding factors such as socioeconomic status, alcohol consumption and cardiovascular disease, the rates of visually significant ARMD in smokers and non-smokers over the age of 75 were calculated in an United Kingdom population-based cross sectional study.[11] Current smokers were twice as likely to have ARMD-related vision loss when compared to non-smokers, ex-smokers had a slightly increased risk (odds ratio of 1.13), and those who had stopped smoking over 20 years earlier were not at increased risk for developing vision loss from ARMD.[11] Genetic susceptibility In addition to increasing one's risk of developing ARMD, certain genetic loci have been associated with variable effects on treatment response, such as intravitreal anti-VEGF agents.[12] Complement factor H (CFH) is an important gene in the pathogenesis of ARMD. Pharmacogenomic studies, such as these, may guide treatment regimens in the future, or may at least provide a more accurate prediction of treatment response. Recently, microRNA dysregulation has been linked with the development of ARMD, modulation of which could provide potential treatments for the disease.[13] Other Risk factors Cardiovascular disease, Hypertension, Female gender, White race[14], Hypercholesterolemia, Obesity, Hyperopia[15], Family History, Light Irides Reference: eyewiki

review.explanation: After age, cigarette smoking is the strongest and most consistently reproduced modifiable risk factor for age-related macular degeneration, roughly doubling the risk of neovascular disease with a clear dose-response relationship and a fall in risk after cessation. It is also the counselling point that matters most, since it is the only major risk factor a patient can change, and it is why smokers should not take beta-carotene in the original AREDS formulation. Hyperlipidaemia and other cardiovascular risk factors have been associated inconsistently across population studies and are not established causal factors; the other accepted associations are family history, white race and complement factor H and ARMS2 polymorphisms.

question: Unilateral rounding of the medial canthal tendon is a feature of which disorder?

options.A: Connective tissue disease involving the medial canthal tendon
options.B: Fracture of the medial wall of the orbit
options.D: Avulsion of the medial canthal tendon

explanation: Categorized: Oclo

review.explanation: The medial canthal angle is normally a sharp, well-defined corner; when the medial canthal tendon is avulsed, typically in a naso-orbito-ethmoid injury, the angle blunts and rounds, the canthus drifts laterally and inferiorly, and traumatic telecanthus with a widened intercanthal distance develops. An isolated medial wall blowout fracture does not by itself detach the tendon, and connective tissue disease does not selectively affect it. A lacrimal sac tumour presents as a firm mass, characteristically extending above the tendon, with epiphora or blood-stained tears, rather than as a rounded canthal angle.

question: Regarding Behcet disease?

options.B: Can have excellent prognosis if treated early

explanation: Categorized: Uveitis Epidemiology It is most common in the Northern Hemisphere in the countries of the eastern Mediterranean and on the eastern rim of Asia, particularly along the ancient Silk Road. Reference: BSC lectures

review.explanation: Behcet disease causes a recurrent, explosive, non-granulomatous panuveitis with an occlusive retinal vasculitis and a mobile, transient hypopyon, and although it usually becomes bilateral over time it can certainly present and remain unilateral, which makes option A the safest true statement. The disease clusters along the ancient Silk Road, in Turkey, the eastern Mediterranean, the Middle East and East Asia, and is distinctly uncommon in people of African descent, so option C is wrong. Historically the visual prognosis has been poor, with a high proportion of eyes losing useful vision within a few years without aggressive immunosuppression.

The key remains the safer choice against the classical teaching of a guarded prognosis, and the item is a good example of a recall that has aged.

question: What type of astigmatism does a patient with a refraction of + 1.00 + 2.00 x 75 degrees have?
explanation: Astigmatism is typically caused by a toric-shaped cornea. Regular astigmatism is present when one meridian of the cornea is the flattest and perpendicular (90 degrees away) from one meridian that is the steepest. With-the-rule astigmatism, the more common type of astigmatism in children, is corrected with a plus cylinder between 60 and 120 degrees. In against-the-rule astigmatism, the astigmatism can be corrected with a plus cylinder between 150 and 30 degrees. Oblique astigmatism is corrected with a plus cylinder between 31 to 59 and 121 to 149 degrees. In irregular astigmatism, the steep and flat meridians of the cornea are not perpendicular to each other. In these patients, cylindrical lenses often do little to improve vision, and rigid gas permeable contact lenses should be tried to reach best vision. One way of classifying astigmatism is by the location of the focal lines within the eye. Simple astigmatism refers to one focal line on the retina and one line either in front of the retina (simple myopic astigmatism) or behind the retina (simple hyperopic astigmatism). In compound astigmatism, both focal lines are either in front of the retina (compound myopic astigmatism) or behind the retina (compound hyperopic astigmatism). In mixed astigmatism, the focal lines are on both sides of the retina (straddling the retina). Transcribed from a screenshot in the source document.

review.explanation: In plus-cylinder notation, with-the-rule astigmatism is corrected with the axis close to 90, conventionally between 60 and 120 degrees, because the cornea is steeper in the vertical meridian; against-the-rule is corrected with a plus axis near 180, meaning 150 to 30, and oblique astigmatism occupies the intervening ranges. This prescription is +1.00 +2.00 x 75, and 75 degrees falls inside the 60 to 120 window, so it is with-the-rule. It is not mixed astigmatism, because both principal meridians are hyperopic, +1.00 D in one and +3.00 D in the other, so both focal lines lie behind the retina.

question: After uncomplicated cataract surgery, patient came to you on 6 th post-operative day, patient has pain, decreased vision and hypopion on examination, most likely this patient has:
explanation: Categorized: Retina TASS generally presents within hours of surgery, while infectious endophthalmitis typically develops 2 to 7 days after surgery. Both entities can cause severe vision loss, corneal edema, and anterior chamber inflammation, even hypopyon. Reference: Self assessment

review.explanation: Acute postoperative endophthalmitis typically declares itself two to seven days after cataract surgery with pain, falling vision, fibrin and hypopyon, and the commonest isolates in the Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study were gram-positive coagulase-negative cocci, chiefly Staphylococcus epidermidis derived from the patient's own lid and conjunctival flora. Toxic anterior segment syndrome appears within 12 to 24 hours, is characteristically painless with limbus-to-limbus corneal oedema, and improves with intensive steroid. Candida and Propionibacterium acnes produce delayed, chronic, low-grade inflammation weeks to months later, so neither fits a florid sixth-day hypopyon.

question: Compared to plasma, human aqueous humor has a relative paucity of which component?
explanation: aqueous humor has an excess of hydrogen, chloride, and ascorbate. It has a deficit of bicarbonate compared to plasma and is essentially protein-free (i.e. 1/200th to 1/500th the protein of plasma) which explains its optical clarity. The relative lack of protein also demonstrates the integrity of the blood-aqueous barrier of the eye. The protein composition of the aqueous includes albumin (~50% of aqueous protein), growth factors, enzymes (e.g. carbonic anhydrase, lysozyme), prostaglandins, cAMP, steroid hormones, catecholamines, and hyaluronic Transcribed from a screenshot in the source document.

review.explanation: Aqueous humour is not a simple ultrafiltrate of plasma; active secretion by the non-pigmented ciliary epithelium gives it an excess of ascorbate (many times the plasma concentration), hydrogen ions, so that it is slightly acidic, and chloride, together with a deficit of bicarbonate and glucose and, above all, of protein, which is a small fraction of the plasma level and accounts for its optical clarity and for the integrity of the blood-aqueous barrier. Bicarbonate is therefore the component present in relative paucity in human aqueous. The high ascorbate is thought to be antioxidant protection for the avascular anterior segment against ultraviolet-generated free radicals.

review.explanation: Duane retraction syndrome is a congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder in which the abducens nucleus and nerve fail to develop, and the lateral rectus is instead innervated by a misdirected branch of the oculomotor nerve intended for the medial rectus. Co-contraction of the two horizontal recti on attempted adduction produces the globe retraction and narrowing of the palpebral fissure that define the syndrome, along with limited abduction and often upshoots or downshoots. The oculomotor nucleus itself is structurally normal; it is merely the source of the aberrant branch, which is why option B is wrong.

question: Anterior communicating artery aneurysm will lead to problem in which
explanation: Categorized: Neuro Intracranial aneurysms are sometimes presented with visual symptoms by their rupture or direct compression of the optic nerve. It is because their prevalent sites are anatomically located close to the optic pathway. Anterior communicating artery is especially located in close proximity to optic nerve. Aneurysm arising in this area can produce visual symptoms according to their direction while the size is small. Clinical importance of visual symptoms presented by aneurysmal optic nerve compression is stressed in this study. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2764022/#:~:text=Intracranial%20aneur ysms%20are%20sometimes%20presented,close%20proximity%20to%20optic%20nerv

review.explanation: The anterior communicating artery lies immediately above the intracranial optic nerves and chiasm, so an aneurysm arising there characteristically compresses the optic nerve or chiasm and produces visual field loss, sometimes a junctional scotoma, well before it ruptures. A painful third nerve palsy with pupil involvement is the signature of a posterior communicating artery aneurysm, and sixth nerve involvement suggests cavernous sinus or basilar disease rather than an anterior circulation aneurysm. Any unexplained optic neuropathy or chiasmal field defect in a young patient warrants imaging that includes vascular sequences for exactly this reason.

question: A patient is suspected to have Propionibacterium acnes endophthalmitis after cataract surgery. What antibiotic is recommended for vitreous injection?
explanation: The intravitreal or endocapsular antibiotic that is appropriate for the treatment of P acnes (a gram-positive anaerobic bacillus) is vancomycin. P acnes endophthalmitis often presents with mild inflammation postoperatively, and the hallmark feature is a whitish intracapsular plaque (or plaques). Suspicion can be confirmed with Gram stain and/or anaerobic cultures, which should be held for at least 2 weeks because P acnes is a slow-growing organism. Although intravitreal or endocapsular injection of vancomycin may initially help, inflammation frequently recurs, and curative therapy often requires vitrectomy, with or without capsulectomy and with or without intraocular lens (IOL) removal. Transcribed from a screenshot in the source document.

review.explanation: Propionibacterium (now Cutibacterium) acnes is a slow-growing gram-positive anaerobic bacillus that causes chronic, delayed postoperative endophthalmitis with mild, often granulomatous inflammation that responds transiently to steroid, and its hallmark is a white intracapsular plaque; anaerobic cultures must be held at least two weeks. Vancomycin is the intravitreal agent of choice for gram-positive organisms including P acnes. Gentamicin covers gram-negatives and carries a real risk of macular infarction intravitreally, and neither moxifloxacin nor trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a standard intravitreal agent. Injection alone is frequently followed by recurrence, so definitive cure often needs vitrectomy with capsulectomy and sometimes IOL removal.

question: Medial canthal tendon is attached to all except Fred oculo ?
explanation: Categorized: Oclo Reference: JEFFREY A. NERAD Papilledema Papilledema refers to ONH edema resulting from increased intracranial pressure (ICP). Papilledema may result from a variety of conditions, including an intracranial mass; hydrocephalus; meningeal processes, such as an infection of the central nervous system (CNS) or infiltration by a granulomatous or neoplastic process; increased venous pressure from cerebral venous thrombosis, venous sinus stenosis, or dural fistula; idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH)

Options A, B and D all name parts of that attachment, D being simply another name for the bone bearing the anterior crest. The orbital plate of the frontal bone forms the orbital roof and has no attachment to the medial canthal tendon, so it is the exception.

question: Which is the least likely to cause neovascular glaucoma ?
explanation: Categorized: Retina Calcification in Retinoblastoma is due to: RPE metaplasia; necrosis

review.explanation: Neovascular glaucoma requires sustained retinal or ocular ischaemia driving VEGF release into the anterior segment. Ischaemic central retinal vein occlusion is the classic cause, accounting for roughly a third of cases, and ocular ischaemic syndrome from severe carotid occlusive disease is another well-recognised one, with rubeosis in a majority of affected eyes. Central retinal artery occlusion does produce rubeosis, but in only a small percentage of eyes. Carotid stenosis on its own, in the absence of the chronic hypoperfusion that defines ocular ischaemic syndrome, is the least direct cause of the four.
review.concern: Debatable item. Carotid stenosis severe enough to matter presents as ocular ischaemic syndrome, so options C and D overlap awkwardly, and central retinal artery occlusion is itself an uncommon cause of rubeosis, well below the rate after ischaemic CRVO. If the examiner intended CRAO as the rare cause, option A would be their answer. I have accepted the key because uncomplicated carotid stenosis without ocular ischaemia does not by itself drive neovascularisation, but I would not defend it strongly.

question: Mom has disease and her brothers too, Mom children are affected but her brothers children are not, this mode of inheritance is:
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Transmission exclusively through affected women, with all children of an affected mother at risk and no transmission at all from affected men, is the signature of mitochondrial inheritance, because the ovum supplies essentially all of the mitochondrial DNA while sperm mitochondria are eliminated. The pedigree described fits exactly: the mother's children are affected while the children of her equally affected brothers are not. X-linked recessive would give carrier daughters through affected men and would not explain affected offspring of both sexes in this pattern, autosomal recessive requires a carrier partner and does not track with the sex of the transmitting parent, and X-linked dominant produces affected daughters of every affected father.

question: Micro-aneurysms in which layer?
explanation: Categorized: Retina Microaneurysms are usually the earliest visible manifestation of diabetic retinopathy. They appear as tiny red dots scattered in the retina posteriorly (single arrows). They may be surrounded by a ring of yellow lipid, or hard, exudates (double arrow). Exudates are the result of vascular leakage, but the specific leaking microaneurysm may not be visible ophthalmoscopically Reference: AAO

review.explanation: Retinal capillary microaneurysms arise from the deep capillary plexus, which lies at the inner border of the inner nuclear layer, so histologically they are found in the inner nuclear layer. This is the same level at which intraretinal dot and blot haemorrhages sit, confined and rounded by the vertically oriented Muller cell processes, whereas nerve fibre layer haemorrhages are flame-shaped because they track along horizontally running axons. Hard exudates, the lipid residue of leakage from those microaneurysms, accumulate in the outer plexiform layer.

question: Copper toxicity all true except:

However, if intraocular copper concentrations return to normal, response amplitude depression can be reversed. Resource: Chalcosis - EyeWiki (aao.org)

review.explanation: Ocular chalcosis from an alloyed copper foreign body causes the sunflower cataract, a Kayser-Fleischer ring of copper deposited in Descemet membrane, and copper deposition on the internal limiting membrane with retinal degeneration, while a nearly pure copper body, above about 85 per cent, provokes a violent sterile suppurative endophthalmitis that can destroy the eye within days. The electroretinogram in chalcosis shows reduced photopic and scotopic amplitudes with delayed implicit times, but these changes can recover once the copper is removed and intraocular levels fall, so describing the flat ERG as irreversible is the false statement.

question: Regarding Bitemporal hemianopia all true except:

options.A: Can be caused by chiasmal lesion
options.B: Patients with unexplained bitemporal hemianopia need MRI

explanation: By exclusion. AION most commonly presented with peripheral island (35%) or sector defect (35%). Visual field defects in AION almost universally showed respect for horizontal meridian, except where only small residual island remained. Inferior altitudinal defect occurred less commonly than expected (18%). PION was more prevalent in our study (31%) compared to others and most often presented with scotoma with or without peripheral defect. Resource: Visual fields in giant cell arteritis | SpringerLink

review.explanation: Bitemporal hemianopia arises from damage to the decussating nasal retinal fibres at the optic chiasm, most often from pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, meningioma or an aneurysm, and because the field loss respects the vertical meridian it localises the lesion precisely. Any unexplained bitemporal defect therefore mandates neuroimaging, preferably MRI with dedicated views of the sella. Giant cell arteritis damages the eye through arteritic anterior, and less often posterior, ischaemic optic neuropathy and through central retinal artery occlusion, producing altitudinal defects that respect the horizontal meridian, central scotomas or profound global loss, never a vertically respecting bitemporal defect, so option C is the exception.

question: Retinal macroaneursm all except:
explanation: RAM is one of the few causes of hemorrhage at multiple levels (preretinal, retinal, and subretinal hemorrhage). patients may be asymptomatic or may complain of acute vision loss due to macular edema or hemorrhage. Also presenting complaint may be floaters due to vitreous hemorrhage. Resource: Macroaneurysm - EyeWiki (aao.org)

review.explanation: Retinal arterial macroaneurysm is one of the few lesions that bleeds simultaneously at several levels, so preretinal, intraretinal and subretinal hemorrhage (and sometimes vitreous hemorrhage) are all classic findings. Chronic leakage from the aneurysm produces macular edema, often cystoid, together with a circinate lipid ring, so CME is expected. Cotton-wool spots are nerve fibre layer infarcts from precapillary arteriolar occlusion and belong to hypertensive, diabetic or vasculitic retinopathy, not to the macroaneurysm itself. Because most of these patients are hypertensive, cotton-wool spots may coexist in the fundus, but they are not a feature of the lesion, so B is the exception.

question: Pseudoexfoliation problem during surgery?
explanation: In the era of phacoemulsification, PXF still represents a relevant challenge for the surgeon. The concurrent presence of poor pupil dilation and zonular weakness is responsible for the increased risk of intraoperative complications that may occur during surgery. Resource: Cataract Surgery in Pseudoexfoliation Syndrome - EyeWiki (aao.org)

review.explanation: Pseudoexfoliation material is deposited on the lens equator and on the zonular insertions and progressively weakens them, so phacodonesis, intraoperative zonular dehiscence, capsular bag instability and late in-the-bag IOL subluxation are the defining surgical hazards; capsular tension rings and careful hydrodissection are the usual countermeasures. Poor pupillary dilatation from deposits on the iris and a rigid pupil compound the difficulty. Corneal edema does occur postoperatively because PXF eyes have reduced endothelial reserve, and PCO can follow any phacoemulsification, but neither is the characteristic intraoperative problem that makes a PXF eye a high-risk case.

question: BRVO recommends:

options.B: Macular edema is treated after 3 months of BRVO

explanation: Resource:

review.explanation: The Branch Vein Occlusion Study protocol was to wait about three months after a BRVO before treating persistent macular edema, because a substantial proportion of eyes improve spontaneously as the hemorrhage and edema settle. Grid laser was then offered only if vision was 20/40 or worse and the fluorescein angiogram showed a perfused, non-ischemic macula, so A is wrong: macular ischemia is a contraindication to macular grid laser, not an indication. Option C is wrong because angiography is deliberately deferred until intraretinal blood clears enough to interpret capillary perfusion, which typically takes longer than four weeks.
review.concern: Answer B reflects the classic BVOS teaching that the exam is testing. Current practice has moved on: anti-VEGF therapy (and dexamethasone implant) is first-line for BRVO macular edema and is started promptly rather than after a three-month observation period.

question: Parents note that their 6 year old boy proptosis over the last year, there are choroidal folds on exam, what to do?
explanation: CT scan or MRI to rule out retro-orbital tumors Resource:

review.explanation: A child with a year of slowly progressive proptosis plus choroidal folds has an orbital mass indenting the posterior globe until proven otherwise, so cross-sectional orbital imaging is the next step; MRI with contrast and fat suppression best characterises soft tissue, defines optic nerve and intracranial extension, and avoids ionising radiation in a child. Choroidal folds are a sign of posterior globe compression or hypotony, not a diagnosis, so fluorescein angiography would merely confirm the folds without explaining them. A Hess chart records the pattern of any motility restriction but does not find the cause. Slowly progressive proptosis at this age suggests optic nerve glioma, dermoid, plexiform neurofibroma or a vascular lesion, whereas rhabdomyosarcoma usually progresses over weeks.

review.explanation: A pontine lesion, classically a hypertensive pontine hemorrhage, interrupts the descending sympathetic fibres travelling through the brainstem to the ciliospinal centre of Budge, so parasympathetic tone is unopposed and the pupils become bilaterally pinpoint while remaining light-reactive (best seen with a magnifier). Mydriasis instead localises to the midbrain and pretectal region, or to a third nerve, ciliary ganglion or pharmacological cause. The useful topographic rule is pons equals small pupils, midbrain equals large or mid-dilated poorly reactive pupils.

question: Toxoplasmosis all except:

options.A: Pyrimethamine is effective and can kill the cysts

explanation: but depends on the other options Treated by triple therapy: Pyrimethamine + sulfazedine + steroid (after 3 days) + folic acid Resource:

review.explanation: No currently available anti-toxoplasma drug eradicates the encysted bradyzoites. Pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, clindamycin, atovaquone and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole all act on the actively dividing tachyzoites only, which is exactly why recurrences arise from cysts at the border of an old pigmented scar. Classic therapy is pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine with folinic acid to protect the bone marrow, and oral corticosteroid added a couple of days after the antiparasitic cover, never as monotherapy. Option B is true: although the typical picture is a single satellite focus beside an old scar, multifocal and bilateral disease is well recognised, particularly in immunocompromised and congenitally infected patients.

question: Regarding SLT, one true:

options.A: Gives marked better results in phakic then pseudophakic

explanation: ? Not sure -SLT laser: 70-100 shots, 3 ns duration -Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) 200-600 30 msec, 1200-2000 shots -It targets trabecular meshwork directly Resource: Ophthalmic Lasers: Settings and Videos - EyeGuru

review.explanation: Selective laser trabeculoplasty delivers sub-millijoule energy in a 3-nanosecond pulse, selectively targeting pigmented trabecular cells without coagulative damage, whereas panretinal photocoagulation delivers on the order of tens of millijoules per burn over 20 to 100 milliseconds to produce a visible retinal burn, so the total energy per application in SLT is far lower. Option C is clearly wrong: the aiming beam is placed directly on the pigmented trabecular meshwork, not posterior to it. Option A overstates the case; SLT works in both phakic and pseudophakic eyes and any difference in response between them is modest and disputed, certainly not a marked superiority in phakic eyes.
review.concern: Strictly, SLT has a very high peak power because its energy is delivered in nanoseconds; the statement is only true if power is read loosely as energy delivered per application, which is how the exam intends it. B is still the only defensible option since A and C are both wrong as written.

question: Corneal blood staining all true except:

options.A: High IOP is a risk factor.
options.B: Starts to resolve from the center first. (from periphery)

explanation: the periphery clears first followed by the center Resource: AAO Reduced IOP is mostly unexpected to be found in all except (in fred retina 37 was w/o except) Choroidal HG.; Choroidal effusion

review.explanation: Corneal blood staining follows a large or prolonged hyphema, and the two permissive factors are raised intraocular pressure and a compromised endothelium, which together allow hemoglobin breakdown products and hemosiderin to enter the stroma, so A is true. Clearance is slow, taking months to years, and it proceeds from the limbus centripetally, so the central cornea is the last area to clear; the statement that it resolves from the centre first is therefore the false one. This peripheral-to-central pattern is what makes deprivation amblyopia a genuine risk in a young child and is one of the arguments for early surgical evacuation of a hyphema once staining begins.

question: Retinitis pigmentosa and deafness occur in all of the following disorders except
explanation: c. Refsum's disease—there is no deafness in this RP variant Transcribed from a screenshot in the source document.

review.explanation: Usher syndrome is defined by retinitis pigmentosa with congenital sensorineural deafness and is the commonest cause of combined deaf-blindness. Alstrom syndrome pairs a cone-rod dystrophy with sensorineural hearing loss, obesity, insulin resistance and dilated cardiomyopathy. Cockayne syndrome combines a pigmentary retinopathy with sensorineural deafness, cachectic dwarfism, photosensitivity and premature ageing. Refsum disease is defined by a cardinal tetrad of retinitis pigmentosa, peripheral polyneuropathy, cerebellar ataxia and raised CSF protein without pleocytosis, caused by phytanic acid accumulation and treated by dietary restriction of phytanic acid and plasma exchange, so on the cardinal-feature reading it is the odd one out.
review.concern: This question is imperfect. Sensorineural deafness and anosmia are well recognised additional features of Refsum disease and are listed as such in standard tables of syndromic RP, so strictly all four options can be associated with hearing loss. C is the defensible answer only because deafness is not part of Refsum's cardinal tetrad, whereas it is a defining feature of the other three.

question: Patient after local anesthesia develops nausea, vomiting, hypotension and bradycardia. These symptoms can be due to all except:
explanation: Brainstem anesthesia: symptoms of difficulty breathing, dysphasia, hypertension, tachycardia, severe shivering, agitation, confusion, or unconsciousness generally occurring within a few minutes of anesthetic administration. Mechanism may be from spread through the optic nerve sheath or foramina of the orbit Resource: AAO All are features of stickler, except: fred retina Retinoschisis.; Pierre Robin anomaly; Marfinoid habitus.

review.explanation: Nausea, vomiting, hypotension and bradycardia after an orbital block is the picture of either central spread of anesthetic or systemic local anesthetic toxicity. Injection into the optic nerve sheath allows subarachnoid spread to the brainstem, producing confusion, contralateral amaurosis, dysphagia, apnea and cardiovascular depression, which is why resuscitation equipment must be available for every retrobulbar block. Inadvertent intravascular injection gives the same cardiodepressant picture with seizures, and anaphylaxis to hyaluronidase gives hypotension with gastrointestinal upset. Excess epinephrine is the pharmacological opposite: beta-1 mediated tachycardia with hypertension, arrhythmia, tremor and anxiety, so it is the one option that cannot generate bradycardia with hypotension.
review.concern: The source answers A on the strength of a passage describing brainstem anesthesia as causing hypertension and tachycardia. An early sympathetic surge is indeed described, but the classic and better documented endpoint of brainstem anesthesia is respiratory arrest with bradycardia and cardiovascular collapse, so option A can produce the stem's syndrome. Epinephrine excess cannot produce bradycardia and hypotension together, which makes C the cleaner exception. The recall is uncertain (the source itself marks option A with a question mark), so treat this as a considered second opinion rather than a correction.

review.explanation: Read this as a spectacle magnification question. A plus spectacle lens worn in front of a hyperopic eye magnifies the retinal image, so the corrected hyperope sees objects appearing larger, while the minus lens of a corrected myope minifies, roughly 2 percent per dioptre at standard vertex distance. That is also why an aphakic spectacle correction produces marked image magnification and why anisometropes get aniseikonia. Contact lenses largely abolish this effect because they sit at the corneal plane.
review.concern: The stem is badly truncated and depends on a figure that cannot be seen, so this is an interpretation rather than a certain reading. Knapp's law is the caveat: in purely axial ametropia, spectacle correction at the anterior focal point gives an image size similar to the emmetropic eye, so the magnification effect is most marked in refractive ametropia.

question: Prognostic factors for choroidal melanoma include all except: fred retina
explanation: Resource: AAO

review.explanation: The established prognostic factors for uveal melanoma are tumour size (largest basal diameter and thickness), cell type (epithelioid cells carry the worst prognosis, spindle A the best), location (ciliary body involvement and anterior tumours do worse than posterior choroidal), extraocular extension, mitotic rate and increasingly the cytogenetic and gene expression profile, above all monosomy 3 and class 2 signature. Degree of pigmentation has been suggested in some series but is not an accepted independent prognostic factor and does not appear in staging or risk stratification, so it is the exception.

review.explanation: Corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment for sarcoid uveitis, given topically, by periocular or intraocular injection, or systemically, and chronic granulomatous uveitis frequently needs prolonged therapy with a slow taper, so long-term steroid is the true statement. Option B is wrong because steroid-sparing immunosuppression (methotrexate, mycophenolate, azathioprine, or anti-TNF agents in refractory disease) is required in a substantial proportion of patients to avoid steroid morbidity. Option A is wrong because diagnosis rests on a compatible clinical picture with tissue biopsy as the gold standard, supported by chest imaging, ACE and lysozyme; gallium scanning is only an ancillary test, useful when the panda and lambda patterns appear.

question: 3rd nerve palsy, except:
explanation: , in AAO, they mentioned it could be painful! Resource: AAO

review.explanation: Taking the stem at face value, all three listed items are recognised features of a third nerve palsy, which is why the recall is unsatisfactory. Aberrant regeneration follows compressive and traumatic palsies, and a dilated poorly reactive pupil is the hallmark of a compressive lesion such as a posterior communicating artery aneurysm. Pain is the least constant feature: it is expected with an aneurysm but is variable in microvascular palsy and absent in many cases, so it is the weakest generalisation and the best answer available.
review.concern: The stem is truncated and probably lost a qualifier. If the original read microvascular or ischemic third nerve palsy, the answer would change: aberrant regeneration never occurs in an ischemic palsy and the pupil is characteristically spared, while pain is common. Answer with caution and treat this item as unreliable.

question: common cause of 3rd nerve palsy in adults:
explanation: The majority of complete or incomplete CN III palsies without pupil involvement are secondary to an ischemic process. Resource: AAO

review.explanation: In adults, especially those over 50 with vasculopathic risk factors, the commonest cause of an isolated third nerve palsy is microvascular ischemia of the nerve trunk, typically pupil-sparing, painful or painless, and resolving over about three months. The vasa nervorum infarct spares the peripherally placed pupillomotor fibres, which is the anatomical basis of the pupil rule. Tumour and trauma are important but far less frequent causes, and aneurysm, although only a minority of cases, is the one that must be excluded urgently whenever the pupil is involved or the palsy is incomplete with pain.

question: Thyogeson's superficial punctate keratopathy is best treated by:
explanation: topical corticosteroids are considered as mainstay treatment for TSPK because they are highly effective in controlling both, the clinical signs and symptoms of the disease, Resource: Thygeson Superficial Punctate Keratitis - EyeWiki

review.explanation: Thygeson superficial punctate keratitis is a chronic bilateral epithelial keratitis with coarse, elevated, greyish-white intraepithelial dots and a quiet conjunctiva, and it responds dramatically to low-potency topical corticosteroid; loteprednol is a good choice because its ester structure carries a lower risk of steroid-induced pressure rise during the prolonged low-dose treatment these patients need. Topical ciclosporin is a legitimate steroid-sparing alternative but is second line and slower to work. Idoxuridine and trifluridine are antivirals with no role here; idoxuridine in particular is epitheliotoxic and was historically used but is now avoided.

question: chronic asymptomatic pt with dacrocystitis, the organism is:
explanation: , B more with acute -Streptococcus pneumonia was the most common isolate in both adult (11 (14.86%)) and pediatric (30 (24.79%)) dacryocystitis. For both pediatric subgroups, gram positive isolates were the major organism (59 (57.84%) for chronic dacryocystitis with NLDO and 12 (63.16%) for acute dacryocystitis). -Streptococcus pneumonia was the leading pathogen for chronic dacryocystitis with NLDO, and Staphylococcus aureus was the leading pathogen for acute dacryocystitis Resource: all resource from articles, I couldn't find anything in books The microbiologic spectrum of dacryocystitis - PubMed (nih.gov)

review.explanation: The classic teaching distinguishes the organisms of acute and chronic dacryocystitis: Staphylococcus aureus (with Streptococcus pyogenes and Haemophilus in children) predominates in acute suppurative disease, whereas Streptococcus pneumoniae is the organism traditionally associated with the chronic, quiet, mucocoele-type dacryocystitis behind a nasolacrimal duct obstruction. With only these two choices, A is the answer.
review.concern: Modern culture series are less tidy: coagulase-negative staphylococci are frequently the commonest single isolate overall, and gram-negative organisms including Pseudomonas are increasingly reported in chronic cases. The pneumococcus association is a teaching convention rather than a fixed microbiological fact.

question: longest local anesthetic agent is:
explanation: VS D Resource:

review.explanation: Bupivacaine is the longest acting of the four; it is highly lipid soluble and protein bound, giving roughly four to twelve hours of akinesia and analgesia, which is why it is commonly mixed with lidocaine for orbital blocks to combine rapid onset with prolonged duration. Lidocaine lasts around one to two hours, and procaine, an ester rapidly hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase, is the shortest acting. Tetracaine is a potent long-acting ester in the spinal setting but in ophthalmology it is used as a surface anesthetic with only about ten to twenty minutes of effect, so it is not a competitor for block duration. Bupivacaine is also the most cardiotoxic of the group, which matters if it enters a vessel.

question: cataract one false:

options.C: It is a common cause of blindness worldwide.

explanation: PSC Symptoms are glare, difficulty seeing in bright light, and near vision is often more affected than distance. Resource: AAO

review.explanation: Posterior subcapsular cataract sits immediately in front of the nodal point on the visual axis, so it degrades vision most when the pupil is small; near work and bright light both constrict the pupil, which is why PSC characteristically impairs near vision and causes glare and haloes more than distance acuity. Nuclear sclerosis behaves the other way round, reducing distance vision first and often improving unaided near vision through a myopic shift (second sight), so A is true. Cataract remains the leading cause of reversible blindness worldwide, so C is true, making B the false statement.

question: Systemic lymphoma is most likely associated:
explanation: VS B? Resource:

review.explanation: For ocular adnexal lymphoma the risk of concurrent or subsequent systemic lymphoma is strongly site-dependent, and the classic gradient runs eyelid highest, then orbit, then conjunctiva lowest, with figures commonly quoted around two thirds for eyelid, about a third for orbit and about a fifth for conjunctiva. Conjunctival lesions are typically the salmon-patch MALT type with the most indolent behaviour, whereas eyelid lesions are more often higher-grade histologies. Whatever the site, systemic workup with imaging, bone marrow examination and oncology referral is mandatory.

question: Blepharospasm, all true except:
explanation: affects males and females equally Resource: AAO

review.explanation: Benign essential blepharospasm is a focal cranial dystonia of the orbicularis oculi (often with corrugator and procerus involvement), so D is true. Like most dystonias it disappears during sleep and is aggravated by stress, bright light and fatigue, so A is true. It is treated medically, with botulinum toxin injection the mainstay and oral agents and myectomy as alternatives, so B is true. It is not commoner in men: benign essential blepharospasm has a clear female predominance of roughly two to three to one, with onset in the fifth to seventh decades, so C is the false statement.

question: Which of the following has the greatest refractive power:
explanation: 40-44 D See pic Resource:

review.explanation: The greatest change in refractive index in the eye occurs at the air to tear film and cornea interface, from about 1.000 to 1.376, and with an anterior corneal radius of roughly 7.8 mm this surface contributes about plus 48 dioptres, the most powerful refracting surface in the eye. The posterior corneal surface passes from cornea to aqueous, a tiny index step, and being concave to the incoming light it contributes about minus 5 to minus 6 dioptres, so the net corneal power is close to plus 43. The lens surfaces lie between aqueous and lens substance with only small index differences and together give about plus 19 dioptres in the unaccommodated eye. This is why small changes in the anterior corneal surface, whether from refractive surgery or from an unstable tear film, have such a large refractive effect.

question: Which is the last muscle to be affected by retrobulbar anesthesia:
explanation: Cranial nerve IV is not affected since it located outside of the muscle cone. Resource: AAO

review.explanation: A retrobulbar injection deposits anesthetic inside the muscle cone, so the nerves lying within the cone, namely the third and sixth nerves, are blocked first and the recti and levator are akinetic early. The trochlear nerve runs outside the muscle cone, entering the orbit through the superior orbital fissure above the annulus of Zinn and travelling along the orbital roof to the superior oblique, so the superior oblique is the last muscle to be affected, and residual intorsion on attempted downgaze is the classic sign of an otherwise complete block. This is also why a truly complete akinesia may require supplementary anesthetic outside the cone.

question: what is the duration of action of Propracaine:
explanation: ? Answered D previously 10 - 20 min, average of 15 " # $ % Resource: multiple resources

review.explanation: Proparacaine (proxymetacaine) 0.5 percent is an ester topical anesthetic with onset within about 20 seconds and a duration of roughly 10 to 20 minutes, so 15 minutes is the best single figure among the options offered. Its practical advantage over tetracaine and benoxinate is that it stings far less on instillation, which is why it is preferred for tonometry, gonioscopy and paediatric examination. Duration is dose-dependent, so repeated drops for a longer procedure extend the effect, at the cost of increasing epithelial toxicity.
review.concern: The published range is 10 to 20 minutes, so both option B and option D can be defended; C is the mid-range figure and the safest choice.

question: The incidence of microscope induced light toxicity can be decreased by:

options.D: Using a coaxial path of light

explanation: Resource: kanski

review.explanation: Operating microscope phototoxicity is a photochemical injury to the RPE and outer retina and its severity is dose-dependent, that is a product of irradiance and exposure duration, so the single most effective and most practical protective measure is to keep the light exposure short and the illumination no brighter than needed. Option D is the opposite of protective: a coaxial beam focuses light directly onto the macula, so tilting the microscope off-axis reduces risk, which also makes C wrong. Option B is nonsense as written since a 200 nm filter is outside the range relevant to the visible and near-UV light involved; the useful measures are ultraviolet and short-wavelength blocking filters, oblique illumination, corneal light shields, an air bubble or opaque disc over the pupil, and lowering the light intensity.

question: The likely head position of a patient with left 6th cranial nerve palsy is:
explanation: The patient may also present with a head turn toward the affected eye, to avoid abduction and thereby minimize diplopia. Resource: AAO

review.explanation: A sixth nerve palsy produces an abduction deficit with uncrossed horizontal diplopia that is worst on gaze towards the paretic side. The patient adopts a compensatory face turn towards the side of the palsy, so that both eyes are moved into the field of gaze away from the paretic muscle's field of action, where the images fuse. A left sixth nerve palsy therefore produces a left face turn. Head tilt is the compensatory posture for a cyclovertical problem, classically the contralateral tilt of a fourth nerve palsy, not for a horizontal rectus palsy.

question: A disease is equally present in boys and girls, found in 1/4 of the family, the parents are not affected. What is the mode of transmission:
explanation: Diseases that are inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern require that both parents of an affected individual carry at least one copy of the disease allele. With AR traits, many individuals in a pedigree can be carriers, probably without knowing it.

review.explanation: Equal involvement of both sexes rules out X-linked recessive inheritance, which predominantly affects males. Unaffected parents rule out autosomal dominant inheritance in a fully penetrant trait, and also exclude mitochondrial inheritance, which is transmitted from an affected mother to all her children. Two carrier parents give a one in four recurrence risk in each pregnancy with both sexes equally affected and characteristic skipping of generations, which is precisely the pedigree described, so this is autosomal recessive. Consanguinity, if present, would strengthen the inference further.

question: Regarding superior oblique, which is false :

options.B: Originates from sphenoid lateral to optic foramenc)
options.D: Intorts the eye from primary position

explanation: originates from the body of sphenoid bone, medial to the origin of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle and superomedial to the optic canal. Resource: AAO

review.explanation: The superior oblique arises from the periosteum of the body of the sphenoid superomedial to the optic canal, close to the origin of the levator, and not lateral to the optic foramen, so B is false as written. Its functional origin, however, is the trochlea on the superomedial orbital rim, from which the reflected tendon runs backwards and laterally to insert under the superior rectus. From that functional origin the tendon makes an angle of about 51 degrees with the visual axis, which is why its primary action in the primary position is intorsion (D true) and why depression becomes its dominant action as the eye adducts (C true in the sense examiners intend).
review.concern: Option A is also false as transcribed: 23 degrees is the angle the vertical recti make with the visual axis, whereas the obliques act at about 51 degrees. The recall probably corrupted this figure, so the item has two false options; B is the anatomically unambiguous one and the intended answer.

question: True about ESR:

options.A: Can be normal in biopsy proven GCA
options.D: An ESR combined with CRP has higher sensitivity than ESR alone

explanation: ? CRP is a more sensitive marker than ESR for a positive TAB that is diagnostic of GCA. There may be clinical utility in obtaining both tests in the evaluation of patients with suspected GCA. A small proportion of patients with GCA may have normal inflammatory markers at diagnosis Resource: published Article - https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3307891/

review.explanation: A normal ESR does not exclude giant cell arteritis: a small but real proportion of biopsy-proven cases have normal inflammatory markers at presentation, which is why a compelling clinical picture (jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, new headache, amaurosis fugax, anterior ischemic optic neuropathy with a chalky white swollen disc in a patient over 50) mandates high-dose steroid and temporal artery biopsy regardless of the blood results. This makes C wrong. B is wrong because ESR is a non-specific acute phase marker raised by infection, malignancy, anaemia, renal disease, pregnancy and simple ageing.
review.concern: Option D is arguably true as well: CRP is the more sensitive single marker and requesting both raises the overall detection rate, which is why current practice is to order ESR, CRP and platelet count together. A remains the classic and safest answer because it carries the clinically important message, but this item has two defensible true statements.

question: Regarding lens, which is true:

options.A: Induction of primary lens fibers at day 49
options.B: Tunica vasculosa lentis has an essential function
options.C: Secondary lens fibers from posterior epithelium
options.D: Tunica vasculosa lentis encloses the lens by week 6

explanation: See pic

review.explanation: The tunica vasculosa lentis, derived from the hyaloid artery system, is the essential nutritional supply of the lens during development, before the aqueous circulation is established; it later regresses, and failure of regression leaves a Mittendorf dot, a persistent pupillary membrane or persistent fetal vasculature. Option C is clearly false because only the primary lens fibres come from the posterior epithelium of the lens vesicle; secondary fibres are laid down continuously throughout life by the equatorial epithelium at the lens bow, and are the reason no lens epithelium exists posteriorly in the adult. Options A and D quote timings that do not fit the standard sequence, in which the lens placode invaginates in the fourth week, the lens vesicle separates from surface ectoderm around day 33, primary fibres fill the vesicle in weeks five to seven, and the tunica fully invests the lens only around the third month.
review.concern: This item depends on a figure that cannot be seen, and the developmental dates quoted in options A and D vary slightly between textbooks, so the elimination of those options is approximate.

question: About the cornea, which is false:

options.C: Stroma is linked to Descemet's by collagen
options.D: Endothelial cells are derived from neural crest.

explanation: , By exclusion all other options are correct Resource: BSC lectures

review.explanation: Bowman's layer is not a basement membrane; it is an acellular condensation of the most anterior stroma made of randomly arranged collagen fibrils, and it has no cells to regenerate it, which is why injury through it leaves permanent scarring. The true basement membrane in that region is the epithelial basement membrane, which lies on top of Bowman's layer and is secreted by the basal epithelial cells. Option C is true because collagen filaments and the interfacial matrix anchor the posterior stroma to Descemet's membrane, and D is true because the corneal endothelium, like the stroma and the anterior chamber angle structures, arises from neural crest.
review.concern: Option A is loosely worded: the stromal collagen that predominates is type I with type V forming heterotypic fibrils and type VI in the interfibrillar matrix, with only small amounts of type III in the normal cornea. Older texts do list types I and III together, so it is usually accepted as true, but B is the unambiguous falsehood.

question: Soft contact lens base curve is held constant, but the lens diameter is increased, one would expect to see:
explanation: increased Lens dimeter = tighter fit lens = limbal injection due to Tight lens syndrome Resource: optometrist ! " # $ %

review.explanation: For a soft lens the sagittal depth, and therefore the tightness of fit, depends on both base curve and diameter, so if the base curve is held constant and the diameter is increased, the lens vaults more and drapes more tightly on the eye. The result is a steep or tight fit with reduced movement and lag, conjunctival indentation and circumlimbal injection, the tight lens syndrome that can progress to hypoxic complications. This makes B, and the loose-fit signs of edge lift and excessive movement, all wrong. Practically, either flattening the base curve or reducing the diameter will loosen such a fit.

question: The presence of an extra digit is referred to as:
explanation: it's Simple definition of polydactyly Resource: AAO

review.explanation: Polydactyly is the presence of a supernumerary digit and is a useful systemic clue in ophthalmic genetics, most notably in Bardet-Biedl syndrome, where it accompanies a rod-cone dystrophy, obesity, hypogonadism, renal disease and learning difficulty. Clinodactyly is curvature of a digit in the coronal plane, brachydactyly is abnormal shortness of the digits, and arachnodactyly is the long spidery digits of Marfan syndrome and homocystinuria, both of which are relevant to ectopia lentis but are the opposite of an extra digit.

question: Regarding functions of the aqueous, all true except:

options.A: Supplies amino acids to the lens.
options.B: Supplies glucose to the corneal epithelium.
options.D: It is a transparent conducting medium.

explanation: ? All other options are correct, maybe B as they mentioned "epithelium" and it supposed to be Posterior part of cornea

review.explanation: Taking the question as the examiners intend it, the aqueous humour is the metabolic supply of the avascular anterior segment structures with which it is in direct contact, principally the lens, the corneal endothelium and the trabecular meshwork; it delivers glucose, amino acids, ascorbate and glutathione and removes metabolic waste. It also maintains intraocular pressure and hence globe shape, and is optically clear so that light passes undisturbed, so options A, C and D describe genuine functions. The examiners treat B as the exception on the grounds that the aqueous nourishes the posterior cornea rather than its epithelium.
review.concern: Physiologically option B is defensible and arguably true: the corneal epithelium obtains most of its glucose by diffusion from the aqueous across the stroma, while it takes oxygen from the tear film and atmosphere. Option D is also probably a garbled transcription of transparent refracting medium. This item is a poor recall and should not be relied on.

question: Which is true about Ehlers-Danlos syndrome:

options.D: It is characterized by short fingers.

explanation: By exclusion

review.explanation: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a heterogeneous group of collagen disorders whose shared hallmarks are skin hyperextensibility, joint hypermobility and tissue fragility with easy bruising and poor wound healing that leaves cigarette-paper scars, so A is a core feature of essentially every subtype. Option D is clearly wrong: the digits are hypermobile and often long, not short. Ocular associations to remember are blue sclerae, thin cornea and keratoconus, angioid streaks, ectopia lentis and, in the kyphoscoliotic type, globe fragility with a risk of rupture after minor trauma.
review.concern: Option C is also true: the kyphoscoliotic type (lysyl hydroxylase deficiency) and dermatosparaxis type are autosomal recessive, although most subtypes including the classical and hypermobile types are autosomal dominant. Kyphoscoliosis in option B is likewise real but confined to one subtype. A is the most universally true statement, but the recall probably altered the wording of the distractors.

question: A major risk factor for the development of bacterial keratitis is:
explanation: The two main causes of bacterial keratitis are: contact lens use, especially extended-wear lenses. And eye injury. Resource: AAO

review.explanation: Contact lens wear is the single largest risk factor for bacterial keratitis in the developed world, particularly extended or overnight wear, poor hygiene, topping up solutions, and exposure of lenses or cases to water; the lens creates hypoxia and epithelial compromise while acting as a biofilm-coated vector, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the characteristic organism in lens wearers. Ocular surface disease and trauma, including vegetative injury, are the other major risks. Tap water matters chiefly as the source of Acanthamoeba in lens wearers rather than as an independent bacterial risk, and systemic bacterial infection and age are not major contributors.

question: Which one of the following statements is incorrect regarding alkali burn:

options.A: Causes the pH of intraocular fluids to fall within seconds of injury.
options.B: Should be irrigated with at least 1 liter of saline or water.
options.C: Is potentially more serious than an equivalent acid injury.
options.D: More serious injury may be presumed if there is a substantial epithelial loss or limbal ischemia.

explanation: by exclusion, All other options are correct Resource: AAO

review.explanation: Alkalis raise the pH of the ocular surface and, because they saponify cell membrane lipids and penetrate rapidly through the cornea, the pH of the aqueous rises within seconds to minutes; a statement that intraocular pH falls is therefore the incorrect one. Acids by contrast coagulate stromal protein, which forms a barrier that limits deeper penetration, so an alkali injury is generally more serious than an equivalent acid injury, making C true. Immediate copious irrigation with at least a litre of saline or water, continued until the pH normalises, is the single most important intervention, and extensive epithelial loss with limbal ischemia (the whitening that predicts limbal stem cell failure) defines a severe grade with poor prognosis.

question: The false statement regarding herpetic anterior uveitis is:

options.A: Bilateral herpetic anterior uveitis is a common presentation.
options.B: Diffuse stellate KPs is a feature.
options.C: Decreased corneal sensation is a feature.
options.D: Attack can last from 1 week to several months.

explanation: by exclusion, All other options are correct Resource: AAO

review.explanation: Herpetic anterior uveitis is characteristically unilateral and recurrent in the same eye, so calling bilateral disease a common presentation is the false statement; bilateral herpetic anterior uveitis should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis or suspicion of immunocompromise. The typical features are raised intraocular pressure with active inflammation, diffuse stellate keratic precipitates that are not confined to Arlt's triangle, patchy or sectoral iris atrophy with distortion of the pupil, and reduced corneal sensation from previous epithelial disease, so B and C are true. Attacks are variable in length and may run from a week to several months, needing topical steroid with antiviral cover.

question: The false statement regarding neural crest:
explanation: waves of neural crest : - 1st wave Endothelial cells formation - 2nd wave Stromal cells formation - 3rd wave Anterior angle structures Resource: BSC Lectures

review.explanation: The corneal epithelium and its basement membrane, along with the lens, the lacrimal gland and the eyelid epidermis, derive from surface ectoderm, not from neural crest, so C is the false statement. Neural crest cells migrate from the crests of the neural folds in the region of the forebrain and midbrain into the periocular mesenchyme in successive waves, forming the corneal endothelium first, then the corneal stroma, and then the anterior chamber angle structures including the trabecular meshwork. Neural crest also contributes the sclera, the choroidal stroma, the iris stroma, the ciliary muscle and the orbital bones and connective tissue, which is why disordered neural crest migration produces the anterior segment dysgenesis spectrum such as Axenfeld-Rieger and Peters anomaly.

question: About the prism alternate cover test, one is false:

options.A: Stacking a 30 and 40 PD base out prism will give an additive effect of 70 PD.
options.B: Vertical and horizontal prisms can be stacked to give an estimate of horizontal and vertical deviation.
options.C: Plastic prism should be held in the frontal plane position to give an accurate measurement.
options.D: High plus lenses cause the measured deviation to be less than the true deviation.

explanation: Resource: opthoquestion Promotion collection 2014 Application of 5% Povidone iodine.; Pre-op administration of topical antibiotics.; Addition of antibiotics to the irrigation solution.; Pre-op administration of intra cameral antibiotic. The optic stalk starts to close over the hyaloid vessels at 5- 6 weeks.; The choroidal fissure is closed by 6 weeks gestation.; Bergmeister's papilla represents nerve tissue at the disc.; Malformed lamina cribrosa causes morning glory syndrome.

review.explanation: Prisms of the same orientation must never be stacked, because the deviation produced is greater than the arithmetic sum, so a 30 and a 40 prism dioptre base-out combination measures considerably more than 70 prism dioptres and will grossly overestimate a large deviation; large angles should be split between the two eyes or measured with a large single prism or prism bar. Perpendicular stacking of a horizontal and a vertical prism is acceptable because their effects are in different planes, so B is true. Plastic prisms are calibrated for the frontal plane position and glass prisms for the position of minimum deviation, making C true, and high plus lenses minify so the measured deviation reads less than the true angle, making D true.

question: Which of the following statements is not correct about vortex veins:

options.A: There are usually about 4-7 in each eye.
options.B: They drain the venous system of the retina.
options.C: They drain the venous system of the choroid and anterior uvea.
options.D: They are visible in posterior segment examination.

explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: The vortex veins drain the entire uveal venous circulation, that is the choroid, ciliary body and iris, and typically number four to seven, one in each oblique quadrant, exiting through the sclera behind the equator where their ampullae are visible on indirect ophthalmoscopy or scleral indentation. The retina drains separately through the central retinal vein into the superior ophthalmic vein or cavernous sinus, so option B is the incorrect statement. Knowing the ampullae positions matters surgically, since damage during scleral buckling, strabismus surgery or drainage of suprachoroidal fluid can cause choroidal congestion or hemorrhage.

question: Computed Axial Tomography (CT) is more helpful than MRI in which condition:
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: CT is superior for bone and for radiopaque or metallic foreign bodies, so orbital fracture is the classic indication, with thin-slice coronal reconstruction showing the orbital floor and medial wall and any entrapped tissue. MRI is better for soft tissue contrast, which is why it is preferred for choroidal melanoma and its extraocular extension, for posterior scleritis, and above all for the posterior fossa and any intracranial lesion, where CT is degraded by bone-hardening artefact. CT is also faster and more accessible in an emergency, and it is mandatory before MRI whenever a metallic intraocular foreign body is suspected.

question: One of the nerves involved in the pupillary reflex:
explanation: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK553169/#:~:text=The%20pupill ary%20light%20reflex%20pathway,the%20LGN%20of%20the%20thalamus.

review.explanation: The efferent limb of the pupillary light reflex runs from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus with the third nerve to the inferior division, then to the ciliary ganglion, where postganglionic parasympathetic fibres travel in the short ciliary nerves to reach the iris sphincter and the ciliary muscle. The afferent limb travels in the optic nerve to the pretectal nuclei with bilateral projection through the posterior commissure, which is why the consensual response exists. The long ciliary nerves carry sympathetic fibres to the dilator and sensation from the cornea, while the lacrimal and frontal nerves are purely sensory branches of the first division of the trigeminal with no pupillary role.

question: The suspensory ligament of the globe also known as:
explanation: , https://eyewiki.aao.org/Suspensory_Ligament_of_the_Eye_(Lockwood's_Ligament)

review.explanation: Lockwood's ligament is the suspensory ligament of the globe, a hammock formed by fusion of the inferior rectus and inferior oblique sheaths with the check ligaments of the medial and lateral recti, supporting the eye from below; it is why the globe does not drop after removal of the orbital floor, and why large inferior rectus recessions can produce lower lid retraction. Whitnall's ligament is the superior transverse ligament that acts as the fulcrum redirecting the levator from a horizontal to a vertical vector. The capsulopalpebral fascia is the lower lid retractor, the analogue of the levator aponeurosis, and the lateral rectus check ligament is only one component of the suspensory system.

question: What is the outer most layer supplied by central retinal circulation:
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: The retinal circulation supplies the inner two thirds of the retina, extending outwards as far as the inner nuclear layer, while the choriocapillaris supplies the outer third by diffusion, namely the outer plexiform layer, outer nuclear layer, photoreceptors and RPE. The inner nuclear layer is therefore the outermost layer served by the central retinal artery, and the outer plexiform layer is the watershed between the two circulations. This explains why a central retinal artery occlusion produces inner retinal whitening with a cherry-red spot from the intact choroidal supply at the foveola, and why paracentral acute middle maculopathy on OCT localises to the deep capillary plexus at the inner nuclear layer border.

question: The true statement about general characteristic of acute inflammation:

options.B: Comprises a cellular followed by a vascular phase.
options.C: May be caused by chemical injury.

explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Acute inflammation is the stereotyped innate response to any tissue injury, and chemical injury is a standard trigger alongside trauma, infection, ischemia, thermal and immunological insults, so C is true. Option A is wrong because acute inflammation is non-specific and antigen-independent, in contrast to the specific adaptive response. Option B reverses the sequence: the vascular phase of transient vasoconstriction followed by vasodilatation and increased permeability comes first, and the cellular phase of neutrophil margination, rolling, adhesion and emigration follows. Option D overstates the timescale, since acute inflammation is measured in hours to a few days and persistence beyond that marks the transition to chronic inflammation with lymphocytes, plasma cells and macrophages.

question: Which of the following best explains accommodation:

options.A: Relaxation of circular muscles of ciliary body results in pupil constriction and therefore helps with accommodation.
options.B: Relaxation of circular muscles of ciliary body results in lens increasing its refractive power.
options.C: The lense decreases its antroposterior diameter therefore increase its refractive power.
options.D: Constriction of the circular muscles of ciliary body results in the lens becoming more globular in shape.

explanation: , contraction of the circular muscles of ciliary body>> relaxation of the zonules>increase the antroposterior diameter of the lens.

review.explanation: Accommodation begins with parasympathetic contraction of the circular fibres of the ciliary muscle, which moves the ciliary body forwards and inwards, slackening the zonules and allowing the elastic lens capsule to mould the lens into a more globular shape with steeper surfaces, a greater anteroposterior thickness and a higher refractive power. This makes D correct and directly contradicts A and B, which invoke relaxation of the circular muscle, the state that flattens the lens for distance. Option C is wrong because the anteroposterior diameter of the lens increases, not decreases, during accommodation. Pupillary miosis and convergence accompany this as the near triad but are not themselves the accommodative mechanism.

question: On entry to the orbit, the Ophthalmic artery turns in what relation relative to the optic nerve:
explanation: The OA enters the orbit through the optic canal, and in most individuals, runs inferolaterally to the optic nerve. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/B978012809324501301

review.explanation: The ophthalmic artery arises from the internal carotid just as it leaves the cavernous sinus and enters the orbit through the optic canal inferolateral to the optic nerve, lying within the dural sheath at that point. Once in the orbit it turns and crosses the nerve, in about four fifths of people passing over it superiorly and in the remainder beneath it, to run forwards along the medial orbital wall towards the trochlea, where it terminates as the supratrochlear and dorsal nasal arteries. Its first and clinically most important branch is the central retinal artery, which enters the nerve about 8 to 15 mm behind the globe.
review.concern: The artery is inferolateral at entry, so option B, lateral, is also partly correct, and if the verb turns is read as referring to its crossing then superior would be the answer instead. The recall is ambiguous, though inferior is the best single choice for its position on entering the canal.

question: A cilioretinal artery contributes to some portion of macular circulation in approximately:
explanation: , a cilioretinal artery is present (20%-25% of eyes). AAO, retina and vitreous page

review.explanation: A cilioretinal artery is a branch of the posterior ciliary circulation that emerges at the temporal disc margin with a characteristic hook and supplies part of the papillomacular bundle and macula, and the figure usually quoted in ophthalmic texts is around 20 to 25 percent of eyes, so 25 percent is the intended answer. Its clinical importance is twofold: it preserves central vision in a central retinal artery occlusion by sparing the macula, and it can itself infarct, producing an isolated cilioretinal artery occlusion, classically in association with a central retinal vein occlusion or with giant cell arteritis.
review.concern: Reported prevalence varies widely between series, from around 15 percent to over 30 percent depending on whether detection was clinical or angiographic, so the exact percentage is soft. Given the options, 25 percent is the closest to the commonly quoted figure.
