question: The earliest signs of malignant hyperthermia include the following except:
explanation: The earliest signs are tachycardia, rise in end-expired carbon dioxide concentration despite increased minute ventilation, accompanied by muscle rigidity, especially following succinylcholine administration. Body temperature elevation is a dramatic but often late sign of MH. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1867813/#:~:text=The%20earliest%20si gns%20are%20tachycardia,often%20late%20sign%20of%20MH.

review.explanation: Malignant hyperthermia, triggered in susceptible patients by volatile anesthetics and suxamethonium, presents earliest with a hypermetabolic picture: a rising end-tidal carbon dioxide despite increased minute ventilation, unexplained tachycardia, tachypnoea, masseter spasm after suxamethonium and generalised muscle rigidity. Fever is a dramatic but characteristically late sign and waiting for it delays treatment, so D is the exception. Management is to stop the trigger, hyperventilate with 100 percent oxygen, give dantrolene without delay, and treat the hyperkalaemia, acidosis, arrhythmias and myoglobinuria. This matters in paediatric ophthalmology because strabismus surgery patients have historically been over-represented in reported cases.

question: Regarding optic tract anatomy all true except:

options.B: Terminates as a root on lateral geniculate nucleus.
options.C: Loop around superior cerebral peduncle in the rostral midbrain.
options.D: Runs lateral to the third ventricle.

explanation: , https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/the-optic-tract

review.explanation: The optic tract runs posterolaterally from the chiasm, sweeping around the cerebral peduncle, and divides near its termination into a larger lateral root ending in the lateral geniculate nucleus and a smaller medial root carrying pupillomotor and retinotectal fibres to the pretectal nuclei and superior colliculus, so options B and C describe it correctly. Its blood supply comes chiefly from the anterior choroidal artery, with contributions from the posterior communicating artery, so A is true. A tract lesion produces an incongruous homonymous hemianopia with a contralateral relative afferent pupillary defect and, in time, band or bow-tie atrophy of the contralateral disc.
review.concern: This item is a weak recall. The optic tract does in fact course lateral to the third ventricle along the wall of the hypothalamus, so option D is not clearly false, and option C is garbled (superior cerebral peduncle is not a standard structure). D is given as the answer only because it matches the key and no option is convincingly wrong.

question: Regarding the angle structures, one is false :

options.A: Sampaolesi's line found along Schwalbe's line.
options.B: Scleral spur is posterior to TM.
options.D: Schwalbe's line is the termination of Descemet's membrane.

explanation: , The Scheie's line (SL) develops by the accumulation of detached iris pigment in Ppigment dispersion. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30527354/#:~:text=The%20Scheie%27s%20line%20(S L)%20develops,a%20pathognomonic%20sign%20of%20PDS.

review.explanation: The Scheie stripe (Zentmayer line) is a band of pigment deposited on the posterior lens capsule at the equator in pigment dispersion syndrome, not a trabecular finding, so C is the false statement. Sampaolesi's line is the wavy band of pigment lying on or just anterior to Schwalbe's line, seen in pseudoexfoliation and in pigment dispersion, so A is true. The scleral spur is the white band posterior to the trabecular meshwork and anterior to the ciliary body band and is the key gonioscopic landmark for grading the angle, so B is true. Schwalbe's line marks the termination of Descemet's membrane and the anterior limit of the trabecular meshwork, so D is true; an anteriorly displaced and prominent Schwalbe's line is posterior embryotoxon.

question: Two parents are both affected with an autosomal recessive disorder, the chance that their offspring get affected is:
explanation: , If you are born to parents who both carry the same autosomal recessive gene, you have a 25% (1 in 4) chance of inheriting the abnormal gene from both parents and developing the disease. https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002052.htm#:~:text=If%20you%20are%20born% 20to,would%20make%20you%20a%20carrier.

review.explanation: If both parents are affected by an autosomal recessive disorder, each is homozygous for the mutant allele and therefore has no normal allele to transmit, so every child must inherit two mutant alleles and every child will be affected. The probability is 1, or 100 percent. The familiar one in four figure applies to the quite different situation of two unaffected heterozygous carriers, which is not what this stem describes. The one caveat, which does not change the answer here, is genetic heterogeneity: if the two parents were affected by mutations at different loci causing a clinically similar phenotype, the children could be unaffected double heterozygotes, but for a single-gene disorder the answer is unambiguously 1.
review.concern: The source answers B, one in four, and its own quoted reference explicitly describes parents who both CARRY the gene, not parents who are both affected. The key has confused affected homozygotes with unaffected carriers. Two affected parents with the same recessive condition transmit it to all offspring, so the correct option is D.

question: All true about accommodation except:
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: During accommodation the ciliary muscle contracts, the zonules relax and the elastic capsule allows the lens to become more globular, so its anteroposterior thickness increases and its equatorial diameter decreases; the anterior surface steepens most, the anterior chamber shallows slightly and refractive power rises. Saying the lens becomes thinner is therefore the exception. Convergence is correct because accommodation, convergence and miosis form the near synkinesis triad driven together, which is the basis of the AC/A ratio and of accommodative esotropia.

question: Which of the following is the most radiosensitive:
explanation: The lens is the most radiosensitive structure of the eye and cataract is a well recognized long-term consequence of radiotherapy https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/B9781416031673500140

review.explanation: The lens is the most radiosensitive structure in the eye because the dividing equatorial epithelial cells are highly susceptible to radiation damage and the abnormal fibres they produce migrate posteriorly and cannot be cleared, giving the characteristic posterior subcapsular cataract; thresholds are low, in the low single-figure gray range, and the latency may be years. The cornea and retina tolerate considerably higher doses, and radiation optic neuropathy and retinopathy occur only at much higher cumulative doses, typically above 50 gray. This is why lens shielding is used during head and neck radiotherapy and why cataract is the commonest long-term ocular consequence of ocular irradiation.

question: Clumps of calcific degeneration and eosionphils at the limbus are:
explanation: , https://eyewiki.aao.org/Vernal_Keratoconjunctivitis

review.explanation: Horner-Trantas dots are the discrete white chalky accumulations of degenerated eosinophils and epithelial debris that sit on the limbus in the limbal form of vernal keratoconjunctivitis, accompanied by gelatinous limbal thickening; they are transient and mark active disease. Arlt's line is the horizontal subconjunctival scar in the upper tarsus of trachoma, Fuchs spot is the pigmented macular scar of pathological myopia after choroidal neovascularisation, and Cogan's is used for a microcystic epithelial dystrophy and for a separate interstitial keratitis with vestibuloauditory disease, neither being a limbal deposit.

question: Which is true about iron deposits in the cornea:

options.A: Fleischer ring is found at the apex of the keratoconus.
options.B: Stocker's line is associated with pterygium.
options.C: Ferry's line is found in front of the trabeculectomy bleb.
options.D: Iron deposition occurs in radial keratotomy.

explanation: , cornea AAO

review.explanation: Stocker's line is the vertical iron line lying in the corneal epithelium just ahead of the advancing head of a pterygium, and its presence indicates that the pterygium is long-standing rather than rapidly growing. Option A is false as written because the Fleischer ring outlines the base of the cone in keratoconus, not its apex, and is best seen with a cobalt blue filter. All these lines share the same mechanism, epithelial iron deposition where the tear film pools against an abrupt change in corneal contour, which is also the mechanism of the Hudson-Stahli line of normal ageing and the Ferry line beside a filtering bleb.
review.concern: As transcribed, options C and D are also true statements: the Ferry line does lie in the cornea adjacent to a filtering bleb, and iron lines are well described after radial keratotomy and other keratorefractive surgery. Only A is definitely false, so the recall has probably altered the distractors; B is nonetheless correct.

question: All can cause astigmatism except:

options.A: Right MR resection and right LR recession.
options.D: A staphyloma extending into the macula.

explanation: , by exclusion

review.explanation: Astigmatism requires a difference in refractive power between meridians of the cornea or lens. Horizontal rectus surgery, particularly resection with its tightening effect on the anterior sclera and cornea, is well documented to induce measurable corneal astigmatism, usually transient. Pellucid marginal degeneration thins the inferior peripheral cornea and produces marked irregular against-the-rule astigmatism with the classic crab-claw topography, and a subluxated lens in Marfan syndrome produces lenticular astigmatism from tilt and from the edge effect of the displaced lens. A posterior staphyloma at the macula distorts the posterior globe wall and produces high axial myopia, with retinal distortion and choroidal thinning rather than a meridional difference in refracting power, so it is the exception.
review.concern: A posterior staphyloma can in principle cause some irregular or oblique astigmatism through posterior segment distortion, so this is the weakest of the four rather than an absolute exclusion. It remains the best answer because the other three are all classic astigmatic causes.

question: Characteristic findings in Aniridia all true except:
explanation: , https://eyewiki.aao.org/Aniridia#:~:text=Individuals%20with%20ani ridia%20characteristically%20have,optic%20nerve%20coloboma%20and% 20hypoplasia.

review.explanation: Corneal-to-lens adhesion is the hallmark of Peters anomaly type II, not of aniridia, so B is the exception. Aniridia, usually from PAX6 mutation, is a panocular disorder in which the iris hypoplasia is only the most visible sign: aniridic keratopathy from limbal stem cell deficiency produces peripheral pannus and conjunctivalisation, glaucoma develops in a large proportion of patients as the rudimentary iris stump rotates over the meshwork, and foveal hypoplasia with nystagmus and optic nerve hypoplasia gives permanently reduced acuity, that is a form of visual deprivation amblyopia. Cataract and lens subluxation are also common, and sporadic cases require renal surveillance for Wilms tumour through the WAGR deletion.

question: The average anteroposterior diameter of a 40 year old lens is:
explanation: About Ophthalmic artery, all are true except:

review.explanation: The crystalline lens measures about 9 to 10 mm in equatorial diameter in the adult, while its anteroposterior thickness grows continuously throughout life because secondary fibres are laid down without any being shed, rising from about 3.5 mm at birth to around 4 mm in the fourth decade and 5 mm or more in old age. At age 40 the lens sits in the 4 to 5 mm band. This lifelong growth, with progressive nuclear compaction and loss of capsular elasticity, is the anatomical basis of presbyopia and of the age-related shallowing of the anterior chamber that predisposes to angle closure.
review.concern: Age 40 lies close to the boundary between options B and C, with quoted mean thickness at that age around 4.0 to 4.3 mm, so the answer depends on the source's figures; C is nonetheless the better fit.

question: All causes ectopia lentis except:
explanation: , https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK578193/#:~:text=Ectopia%20lentis%2 0is%20the%20familial,vitreous%20cavity%2C%20or%20retinal%20surface.

review.explanation: Myotonic dystrophy is associated with the polychromatic Christmas-tree cataract, ptosis and pigmentary retinopathy, but not with lens dislocation, so it is the exception. The classic causes of ectopia lentis are Marfan syndrome (typically superotemporal displacement with intact zonules), homocystinuria (inferonasal), Weill-Marchesani, sulfite oxidase and molybdenum cofactor deficiency, hyperlysinaemia, aniridia and ectopia lentis et pupillae. Ehlers-Danlos is a recognised though uncommon cause because of the underlying connective tissue and zonular defect, so it cannot be the intended exception.

question: The corneal epithelium is derived from which of the following:
explanation: , https://eyewiki.aao.org/Embryology_of_the_Eye_and_Ocular_Adnexa

review.explanation: Surface ectoderm gives rise to the corneal and conjunctival epithelium, the lens, the lacrimal and meibomian glands and the eyelid epidermis. Neuroectoderm gives rise to the retina, RPE, optic nerve, pigmented and non-pigmented ciliary epithelium and iris epithelium including the sphincter and dilator muscles. Neural crest supplies the corneal stroma and endothelium, trabecular meshwork, iris stroma, sclera, choroidal stroma and most orbital connective tissue, while true mesoderm contributes only the extraocular muscles and vascular endothelium.

question: Patient with primary ocular melanocytosis, repeated biopsy showed changes.. with no Atypia, the risk of conjunctival malignancy is:
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Melanocytic conjunctival proliferation without atypia on histology carries essentially no risk of progression to melanoma, which is why the answer is zero. Risk stratification in primary acquired melanosis depends entirely on the presence and character of atypia: without atypia the lesion behaves as benign hyperpigmentation, whereas with atypia the risk rises substantially and is highest when epithelioid cells or full-thickness (pagetoid) epithelial involvement are present. The high percentages offered as distractors correspond to severe atypia, not to a biopsy read as free of atypia.
review.concern: The stem says ocular melanocytosis, which is a congenital episcleral and uveal melanocytic condition that does not involve the conjunctival epithelium at all; the biopsy wording indicates the intended entity is primary acquired melanosis. Either reading gives the same answer of zero for conjunctival malignancy.

question: Base line assessment of Thyroid eye disease all except:
explanation: , not included in the base line assessment https://eyewiki.aao.org/Thyroid_Eye_Disease#Signs

review.explanation: Colour vision, pupil testing for a relative afferent defect and eyelid position (margin-reflex distance, lid retraction, lagophthalmos) are all core elements of the baseline thyroid eye disease assessment, the first two because compressive optic neuropathy is the sight-threatening complication that must be excluded at every visit. Intraocular pressure in primary gaze is a routine measurement rather than a disease-specific baseline element, which makes it the odd one out. Standardised assessment schemes such as VISA and the EUGOGO clinical activity score are built around vision, inflammation, motility and appearance/exposure, not on primary-gaze tonometry.
review.concern: The option is awkwardly worded. Intraocular pressure does matter in thyroid eye disease, but the teaching point is that it should be measured in primary gaze AND upgaze, since a rise on elevation reflects restrictive inferior rectus myopathy. Answer C is correct only by elimination, as the other three are unambiguously part of the baseline exam.

question: Which of the following is the most common site of metastasis in ocular melanoma:
explanation: The liver is the most common site of metastatic disease https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2699810/

review.explanation: Uveal melanoma spreads haematogenously because the uvea has no lymphatics, and the liver is by far the dominant target, involved in roughly nine out of ten patients who develop metastatic disease. Lung and bone follow at much lower frequency, and brain metastasis is uncommon. Preauricular nodes are wrong for uveal melanoma since lymphatic spread is a feature of conjunctival and eyelid melanoma, not intraocular melanoma. This hepatotropism is why surveillance protocols centre on liver imaging and liver function testing.

question: A patient has a wide distance between his medial canthi with normal inter- pupillary distance. The correct term to describe this is:
explanation: , https://eyewiki.aao.org/Telecanthus#:~:text=The%20average%20interpupilla ry%20distance%20is,inter%2Dpupillary%20distance%20is%20normal.

review.explanation: Telecanthus is an increased distance between the medial canthi with a normal interpupillary distance and normal orbital position, usually from long or displaced medial canthal tendons, as in blepharophimosis syndrome or after naso-orbito-ethmoid fracture. Hypertelorism means the bony orbits themselves are laterally displaced, so the interpupillary distance is also increased. Exorbitism describes shallow orbits with globe prominence, as in Crouzon syndrome. The normal interpupillary distance in this stem is the discriminating detail that excludes hypertelorism.

question: Features of Neurofibromatosis type 1 include all EXCEPT:
explanation: , type 2 not 1 https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/conditions-and- diseases/neurofibromatosis/neurofibromatosis-type-2 Behcet's disease.; Sarcoidosis.; Brucellosis.; Inflammatory bowel disease.

review.explanation: Bilateral vestibular (acoustic) schwannoma is the defining feature of neurofibromatosis type 2, not type 1, so it is the exception. Neurofibromatosis 1 features include Lisch nodules (iris melanocytic hamartomas, present in most adults), optic pathway glioma, plexiform neurofibroma of the eyelid, and sphenoid wing dysplasia producing pulsatile proptosis without a bruit. Meningioma is far more characteristic of type 2 but is also reported in type 1, so it is a weaker exception than the bilateral acoustic neuroma, which is essentially pathognomonic of type 2.

question: Degeneration of which retinal cell is the principle cause of Retinitis Pigmentosa:
explanation: the final common pathway appears to be photoreceptor cell death by apoptosis (rods followed by cones). https://eyewiki.aao.org/Retinitis_Pigmentosa#Pathophysiology

review.explanation: Retinitis pigmentosa is primarily a rod photoreceptor dystrophy, which explains the classic clinical triad of nyctalopia, progressive ring and then peripheral field loss, and a markedly reduced or extinguished scotopic ERG early in the disease. Cone dysfunction and central acuity loss occur later as a secondary phenomenon. The pigmentary bone-spicule changes reflect RPE migration into the retina after photoreceptor loss, so RPE change is a consequence rather than the primary event in most genotypes. Ganglion cells are relatively preserved, which is the rationale behind retinal prosthesis and gene-therapy strategies.

question: Findings associated with SCA all except:
explanation: Findings in SCR: https://eyewiki.aao.org/Sickle_Cell_Retinopathy https://eyewiki.aao.org/Sympathetic_Ophthalmia#:~:text=Dalen%2DFuchs %20nodules%2C%20which%20are,appear%20thickened%20with%20nod ular%20infiltrations.

review.explanation: Dalen-Fuchs nodules are collections of epithelioid cells and lymphocytes between Bruch membrane and the RPE seen in sympathetic ophthalmia and in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease, and have nothing to do with sickle cell disease. The genuine sickle findings are salmon-patch intraretinal haemorrhage, iridescent spots (resolved haemorrhage in a retinoschisis cavity), black sunburst chorioretinal scars, and peripheral sea-fan neovascularisation at the border of perfused and non-perfused retina in proliferative sickle retinopathy. Comma-shaped conjunctival vessels and angioid streaks are the other associations worth remembering.

question: Patients with HLA B27 has higher incident of the following compared to general population:
explanation: Anterior uveitis (AU) is present in up to 90% of cases of uveitis and approximately 50% of all patients with acute AU (AAU) are human leukocyte antigen B27 (HLA B27) positive. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7813675/#:~:text=Anterior%20uveitis% 20(AU)%20is%20present,(SpA)%20(6).

review.explanation: HLA-B27 is strongly associated with acute anterior uveitis, characteristically unilateral, recurrent, alternating, with intense fibrin and a tendency to hypopyon, and often accompanied by ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis or inflammatory bowel disease. Roughly half of all acute anterior uveitis is HLA-B27 positive, a large excess over the background population prevalence of the allele. Posterior, intermediate and panuveitis have different HLA and disease associations (for example HLA-A29 with birdshot chorioretinopathy), and B27 does not raise their incidence.

question: True about signs & symptoms of posterior vitreous detachment:

options.B: Flashes and floaters are more serious than floaters alone.
options.C: Pigmented cells in anterior vitreous considered high risk for retinal pathology.
options.D: Floaters always signify posterior vitreous detachment.

explanation: , Schaffer's Sign (Tobacco Dust Sign)

review.explanation: Pigmented cells in the anterior vitreous, the Shafer or tobacco-dust sign, represent RPE cells liberated through a full-thickness retinal break and are the single most useful bedside predictor of a retinal tear in acute posterior vitreous detachment, with a positive predictive value around ninety percent. Flashes alone do not prove a tear, since photopsia is generated by vitreoretinal traction that may resolve without a break, so option A is wrong. Floaters may equally arise from vitreous haemorrhage, vitritis, asteroid hyalosis or an isolated Weiss ring without a complete detachment, so option D is wrong. Option B is a soft comparative claim that is broadly reasonable but is not the definitive teaching point of this item.
review.concern: I disagree with the recorded key of B. The source explanation itself reads only Shafer sign (tobacco dust sign), which is the content of option C, so the letter looks like a transcription slip or the options were reordered during extraction. The examinable, textbook-true statement here is the one about pigmented anterior vitreous cells. Option B is not clearly false, which makes this a flawed item, hence medium rather than high confidence.

question: Causes of photoreceptors atrophy include all EXCEPT:
explanation: , https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3871865/, I found CRAO leads to photoreceptors atrophy not CRVO. -not 100% sure.

review.explanation: The photoreceptors and outer retina are nourished by the choriocapillaris, while the inner retina is supplied by the retinal circulation, and this dual supply is the key to the question. Central retinal vein occlusion damages the inner retina, producing inner retinal oedema and later inner retinal atrophy, with the photoreceptor layer relatively preserved, so it is the exception. Retinal detachment separates photoreceptor outer segments from the RPE and causes outer segment degeneration within days. Retinitis pigmentosa is a primary photoreceptor dystrophy, and sclerosis or atrophy of the choroidal vessels starves the outer retina directly, as seen in choroideremia, gyrate atrophy and geographic atrophy.

question: Metastatic calcification associated with all the following except:
explanation: , HYPERparathyroidism, not Hypoparathyroidism https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/metastatic- calcification#:~:text=Metastatic%20calcification%20is%20caused%20by,8%2D

review.explanation: Metastatic calcification is deposition of calcium in previously normal tissue driven by an elevated serum calcium or calcium-phosphate product, so it requires hypercalcaemia. Hypoparathyroidism produces hypocalcaemia and is therefore the metabolic opposite of what is required; hyperparathyroidism is the classic cause. Hypervitaminosis D increases gut calcium absorption and sarcoidosis raises calcitriol through macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, so both cause hypercalcaemia and metastatic calcification, typically manifesting in the eye as calcific band keratopathy. Contrast this with dystrophic calcification, which occurs in already damaged tissue with normal serum calcium, as in phthisis bulbi, optic disc drusen and necrotic retinoblastoma.
review.concern: The item is imperfect because uveitis is also a poor fit: band keratopathy in chronic uveitis such as juvenile idiopathic arthritis is dystrophic rather than metastatic calcification. Hypoparathyroidism remains the cleaner exception because it is incompatible with the hypercalcaemia that defines metastatic calcification, but a strict pathologist could argue for uveitis as well.

question: 36). Macular hole can be caused by :
explanation: , https://eyewiki.aao.org/Macular_Hole

review.explanation: High myopia is a well-recognised cause of secondary macular hole, arising from a combination of posterior staphyloma, myopic foveoschisis and tangential vitreoretinal traction, and it is the setting in which macular hole retinal detachment occurs. Diabetes typically produces cystoid macular oedema and, if a cyst ruptures, a lamellar rather than a full-thickness hole, so it is a much weaker association. Epiretinal membrane characteristically produces a pseudohole or a lamellar hole because the tissue is displaced rather than lost, although a contracting membrane can occasionally lead to a true hole. The commonest cause overall remains idiopathic anteroposterior and tangential traction at the fovea during perifoveal vitreous separation.
review.concern: The stem is truncated (it begins with a stray item number) and only three options were recalled, so the intended discriminator may have been lost.

question: How can we decrease the risk of sympathetic ophthalmia:
explanation: by AAO(see the images below) but have a look in this research https://www.researchgate.net/publication/51604517_Sympathetic_ophthalmia_E nucleation_or_evisceration Enucleation is not found to be the best protective measure against development of sympathetic ophthalmia, as it was thought to be, since there are ample reports of sympathetic ophthalmia occurring not just after evisceration but also after enucleation. The cosmetic outcome of evisceration as opposed to enucleation is found to be better. https://www.researchgate.net/publication/51604517_Sympathetic_ophthalmia_Enucleation_or_e visceration

review.explanation: Enucleation removes the entire uveal tract, which carries the antigens that drive the autoimmune granulomatous response, whereas evisceration leaves uveal tissue behind at the scleral emissaria and around the optic nerve. For that reason enucleation of a blind, badly injured eye, ideally within the first two weeks, remains the standard prophylactic recommendation against sympathetic ophthalmia. Evisceration gives a better cosmetic and motility result and its true risk is very low, which is why some surgeons prefer it, but it is not the answer to a question about minimising sympathetic ophthalmia risk.
review.concern: Worth knowing the nuance the source raises: sympathetic ophthalmia has been reported after enucleation as well, and the absolute risk difference is small, so many surgeons now offer evisceration when the globe is not ruptured. The classic examinable answer is still enucleation.

question: Peripheral rheugmatogenous retinal detachment can be seen with:
explanation: ,B can lead to RRD Ophtha Qs: increased risk for retinal tear and subsequent detachment including cystic retinal tufts, zonular traction retinal tufts,; lattice degeneration,; meridional folds,

review.explanation: Lattice degeneration is the classic peripheral vitreoretinal degeneration predisposing to rhegmatogenous detachment, present in roughly eight percent of the population and found in about a third of eyes with rhegmatogenous detachment. The mechanism is retinal thinning within the lesion with firm vitreous adhesion at its margins, producing atrophic holes within the lattice and horseshoe tears at its posterior and lateral edges during posterior vitreous detachment. Cystic retinal tufts are also a genuine cause of tractional horseshoe tears and account for a minority of phakic detachments, so both options are true, but lattice is by far the stronger and intended association.
review.concern: Only two options were recalled and both are legitimate causes of peripheral rhegmatogenous detachment; lattice is the best answer by strength of association rather than by exclusion of the alternative.

question: All the following diseases are characterized with lymphocytic infiltration EXCEPT:
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Vitreous haemorrhage is an accumulation of red blood cells with a later macrophage and ghost-cell response, not a lymphocytic infiltrate, so it is the exception. Demyelinating optic neuritis shows perivascular lymphocytic cuffing with demyelination. Thyroid eye disease shows lymphocytic and mononuclear infiltration of the extraocular muscle interstitium with glycosaminoglycan deposition, sparing the muscle fibres themselves. Sjogren syndrome is defined histologically by focal lymphocytic sialadenitis and dacryoadenitis, and the focus score on minor salivary gland biopsy is part of the classification criteria.

question: Pediatric Ophthalmology: Which is false about Duane's type 1:

options.B: Widening of the palpebral fissure on abduction.
options.C: It most often involves the left eye.
options.D: Causes facial turns to the opposite side.

explanation: , Head turns to the involved Side (type 1 type 2،,3=to the opposite side. AAO.

review.explanation: In Duane syndrome type 1 the head turn is toward the affected side, not away from it, because turning the face toward the side of the limited abduction places the eyes in adduction where fusion is possible; that makes option D the false statement. Type 1 is defined by limited abduction with relatively normal adduction, from aberrant innervation of the lateral rectus by the oculomotor nerve with absence of the abducens nucleus. Co-contraction of the horizontal recti on adduction retracts the globe and narrows the palpebral fissure, so the fissure conversely widens on attempted abduction, making option B true. The left eye and female sex are the recognised predilections, so option C is also true.

question: A 5 year old child presents with 20/200 VA OU, Cycloplegic refraction = + 8.50. Pinhole no improvement. Your first step would be:

options.A: Take MRI scan of the head.

explanation: , amblyogenic number iso-hyperopia >4.00

review.explanation: This is bilateral isoametropic amblyopia from uncorrected high hyperopia, and the first and essential step is optical correction of the full cycloplegic refraction. Hyperopia above about five dioptres is amblyogenic, and a five-year-old has enough residual accommodation that under-correction leaves a persistently blurred retinal image and no stimulus for visual maturation. Neuroimaging is not indicated when the reduced acuity is fully explained by a large refractive error and pinhole fails to improve it (a pinhole often does not help in dense bilateral amblyopia). Delaying a month wastes treatment time within the sensitive period; acuity should instead be rechecked after several weeks of spectacle wear, since much of the gain comes from optical treatment alone before any occlusion is added.
review.concern: Some clinicians symmetrically reduce a very large hyperopic correction to encourage accommodative effort, but that applies to non-amblyopic children; with established bilateral amblyopia the full cycloplegic correction is the standard first step.

question: All about ocular examination findings in Crouzon syndrome is true except:
explanation: https://eyewiki.aao.org/Craniosynostosis_Syndromes#:~:text=The%20most%20c ommon%20ophthalmic%20manifestations,atrophy%20secondary%20to%20chro nic%20papilledema.

review.explanation: Aniridia is a PAX6-related panocular malformation with foveal and optic nerve hypoplasia, glaucoma and limbal stem cell deficiency, and is not part of Crouzon syndrome, so it is the exception. Crouzon syndrome is a craniosynostosis from FGFR2 mutation producing shallow orbits with exorbitism, hypertelorism, V-pattern exotropia and other strabismus from orbital dysmorphism and extraocular muscle anomalies, and exposure keratopathy that can progress to corneal ulceration. Optic atrophy is common and follows chronic papilledema from raised intracranial pressure, or direct optic canal narrowing.

question: A preterm infant, GA= 27 weeks, BW= 950 grams admitted to NICU, when should this infant have his initial retinal exam to screen for ROP:
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

referenceLinks.title: Retinopathy of Prematurity - EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: US screening criteria (birth weight <=1500 g or gestational age <=30 weeks) and the full table of postmenstrual age at first exam by gestational age at birth (22 weeks GA -> 31 weeks PMA), plus a fundus photograph of dragged vessels and macular fold from untreated ROP

figureFinding: ROP screening: timing of the initial dilated retinal examination for a 27-week, 950 g preterm infant (31 weeks postmenstrual age or 4 weeks chronologic age, whichever is later)

review.explanation: Screening timing is driven by postmenstrual age for the most premature infants: for a gestational age of 22 to 27 weeks the first examination is at 31 weeks postmenstrual age, while for 28 weeks and above it is at four weeks chronological age. At 27 weeks gestation, 31 minus 27 gives four weeks of chronological age, which falls in the four to six week window. Examining immediately or at one to two weeks is too early, because ROP has not yet developed and the examination stresses a fragile neonate for no yield; waiting eight to ten weeks risks missing the treatment window for type 1 disease. This infant qualifies for screening on both criteria, since the thresholds are gestational age 30 weeks or less or birth weight 1500 g or less.

question: Most common cause of unilateral proptosis in children is:
explanation: The most common cause of proptosis in children is orbital cellulitis followed by malignant conditions like rhabdomyosarcoma, retinoblastoma, lymphoma, ewings sarcoma and metastasis. https://srjhs.org/unilateral-proptosis-in-a-child-need-for-prompt- diagnosis/#:~:text=The%20most%20common%20cause%20of,vascular%20malformation s%20and%20developmental%20anomalies.

review.explanation: Orbital cellulitis, usually secondary to ethmoid sinusitis in a child, is the commonest cause of acute unilateral proptosis in childhood and far outnumbers all tumours combined. The clinical picture of fever, lid oedema, restricted and painful motility and a raised white count distinguishes it. Rhabdomyosarcoma is the commonest primary orbital malignancy of childhood and is the classic answer for rapidly progressive proptosis over days to weeks without infective signs, while capillary haemangioma is the commonest benign orbital tumour of infancy. Leukaemic infiltration and metastatic neuroblastoma are much less common and often bilateral or associated with systemic signs.

question: A child with orbital mass changing in size, what is the most probable diagnosis:
explanation: Exacerbations tend to occur during URTI and may be managed with a short course of systemic corticosteroids. Rapid expansion may be seen in cases of intralesional hemorrhage. A hyperopic patient is sliding his glasses down his nose, he is:

review.explanation: Fluctuation in size is the signature of lymphangioma: the lesion enlarges during upper respiratory tract infection as the lymphoid follicles within it react, and can expand abruptly from spontaneous intralesional haemorrhage into a chocolate cyst. Imaging shows a poorly circumscribed, multicystic infiltrative lesion with fluid-fluid levels, and it does not fill on contrast because it lacks a significant arterial supply. Rhabdomyosarcoma grows rapidly and relentlessly rather than waxing and waning, and is a surgical emergency for biopsy. Capillary haemangioma is the other lesion that changes acutely, swelling with crying or Valsalva, but its natural history is proliferation in infancy followed by involution.

question: A child with anisometropia, what is your plan: Give full correction. Partial correction. Treat as if it is amblyopia. Incomplete. To assess lacrimal outflow:
explanation: Dr.faky's lecture.

review.explanation: The question that matches these options is how to assess lacrimal outflow, and the answer is the fluorescein dye disappearance test: fluorescein is instilled and the tear meniscus is inspected after about five minutes, with persistent dye indicating delayed drainage. Schirmer testing measures aqueous tear production, not drainage. Tear break-up time assesses tear film stability and the lipid layer. Rose bengal (or lissamine green) stains devitalised epithelium and mucin-deficient areas in ocular surface disease. Jones I and II dye tests and irrigation are the next steps to localise the level of obstruction.
review.concern: The stored stem is contaminated: it begins with a fragment of a different question about managing anisometropia in a child, then the real stem (to assess lacrimal outflow) follows. The options belong unambiguously to the lacrimal outflow question, so the item is answerable, but the record should be cleaned.

question: Factor helpful in determining the type of ptosis:
explanation: No explanation was provided in the source document.

review.explanation: Levator function, measured as upper lid excursion from downgaze to upgaze with the brow immobilised, is the measurement that separates the categories of ptosis and drives surgical planning: good function (8 mm or more) suggests aponeurotic ptosis and permits levator advancement, fair function allows levator resection, and poor function (4 mm or less), as in congenital myogenic ptosis or blepharophimosis, requires frontalis suspension. Margin-reflex distance and palpebral fissure height quantify the severity of the droop but do not distinguish its mechanism. Bell phenomenon is assessed to gauge the risk of postoperative exposure keratopathy, not to classify the ptosis.

question: Patients with Myesthenia Gravis may have all the following except:
explanation: , the pupils are never involved in MG. https://eyewiki.aao.org/Myasthenia_Gravis#Signs

review.explanation: Myasthenia gravis affects striated muscle at the nicotinic neuromuscular junction and therefore never involves the pupil, which is smooth muscle under muscarinic autonomic control; a relative afferent pupillary defect indicates asymmetric optic nerve or extensive retinal disease and is the exception. Variable, fatigable ptosis worse at the end of the day, with Cogan lid twitch and enhancement of ptosis on sustained upgaze, is the commonest presentation. Painless variable diplopia from any pattern of ocular misalignment, including a pseudo-internuclear ophthalmoplegia, is typical. Bulbar involvement with dysphagia, dysarthria and respiratory weakness defines generalised disease and matters because of the risk of myasthenic crisis.

question: A lesion of the upper posterior aspect of the right occipital lobe is most likely to affect which quadrant of the visual field in the left eye:
explanation: the image described the opposite, just imagine the reverse ^_^.

referenceLinks.title: Homonymous Superior Quadrantanopia - StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf)
referenceLinks.shows: The retinotopic rule this question tests - dorsal fibers carrying the inferior visual field terminate on the superior lip of the calcarine fissure, ventral fibers carrying the superior field on the inferior lip; so a lesion above the calcarine gives an inferior quadrantanopia

referenceLinks.title: Homonymous Hemianopsia - StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf)
referenceLinks.shows: Multiple visual-pathway schematics mapping lesion site to field defect, including retrochiasmal/occipital lesions and why occipital defects are highly congruous

referenceLinks.title: Crossed Quadrant Homonymous Hemianopsia - EyeWiki
referenceLinks.shows: Humphrey perimetry printout of quadrantic homonymous defects plus occipital infarct MRI; illustrates defects that respect the vertical midline and the above-vs-below calcarine relationship

figureFinding: Right occipital lobe lesion ABOVE the calcarine fissure (cuneus) -> left inferior homonymous quadrantanopia; in the LEFT eye this is the lower temporal quadrant

review.explanation: A right occipital lesion produces a left homonymous field defect, and the retinotopic map is inverted, so the upper bank of the calcarine fissure (the cuneus) represents the inferior visual field. An upper right occipital lesion therefore gives a left inferior quadrantanopia. In the left eye the left half of the visual field is the temporal field, so the affected quadrant is the lower temporal one. The posterior location adds that the defect is congruous and involves central field, since the occipital pole carries macular representation.

question: What is true about MRI:

options.C: It is used to see the orbital part of the optic nerve.

explanation: https://radiopaedia.org/articles/demyelination-protocol mri#:~:text=MRI%20protocol%20for%20demyelinating%20diseases,ischemic%20o r%20toxic%20in%20origin.

review.explanation: MRI is the modality of choice for demyelination because of its soft tissue contrast; FLAIR sequences show periventricular ovoid lesions perpendicular to the ventricles (Dawson fingers), and gadolinium enhancement distinguishes active from old plaques, which is what determines risk of conversion to multiple sclerosis after optic neuritis. Bone is essentially signal-void on MRI and CT is the correct study for orbital fractures and bony detail, so option A is wrong. Metallic intraocular foreign body and pacemakers are the practical contraindications to remember.
review.concern: Option C is also true as written: MRI with fat-suppressed T1 and gadolinium is in fact the best modality for the orbital segment of the optic nerve. The item is therefore flawed, but B is the intended and strongest answer since the sensitivity of MRI for demyelination is the classic teaching point.

question: All are early signs of glaucoma except:
explanation: ? see the image below from AAO

review.explanation: The earliest detectable structural change in glaucoma is loss of retinal nerve fibre layer, which can precede visible disc change and reliable field loss by years and is the basis of OCT-based early diagnosis. Disc (Drance) haemorrhage crossing the rim at the disc margin is a well-known early sign and a strong predictor of subsequent progression. Beta-zone peripapillary atrophy is associated with glaucomatous damage and its progression. Vertical elongation of the cup reflects preferential loss at the superior and inferior poles, and by the time the cup has visibly elongated a measurable amount of rim tissue has already been lost, which is the presumed logic of the key.
review.concern: This item is genuinely ambiguous and the source itself flags uncertainty. All four options appear in standard lists of glaucomatous optic disc and nerve fibre layer change, and vertical elongation of the cup is widely taught as an early sign, so the key is hard to defend on principle. If any option is the odd one out, peripapillary atrophy is arguably the least specific to glaucoma, since it is common in myopia and normal ageing. I cannot confidently overturn the key, so treat this recall as unreliable rather than as a fact to memorise.

question: Pigments in the angle are seen in all except:
explanation: , A Pseudo-exfoliation Syndrome patient, cataract extraction would be difficult because:

review.explanation: Prostaglandin analogues increase melanin content within existing iris stromal melanocytes and cause periocular skin darkening and eyelash growth, but they do not liberate pigment into the aqueous or deposit it in the trabecular meshwork, so they are the exception. Pigment dispersion syndrome produces a dense homogeneous band of trabecular pigment from iris pigment epithelium rubbed off by lens zonules, with a Krukenberg spindle and mid-peripheral iris transillumination. Pseudoexfoliation gives patchy trabecular pigmentation plus the pigment line anterior to Schwalbe line (Sampaolesi line). Laser iridotomy and trabeculoplasty both release pigment acutely into the angle, which is why an intraocular pressure spike can follow.

question: The following are associated with high risk of developing glaucoma:
explanation: recessions greater than 180° are associated with a 4-9% incidence of glaucoma. https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1204999- overview#:~:text=Glaucoma%20after%20angle%20recession%20of,have%20ocula r%20injuries%20each%20year.

review.explanation: Angle recession involving 180 degrees or more of the circumference is the classic high-risk finding for late-onset traumatic glaucoma, which arises from scarring and dysfunction of the trabecular meshwork and may appear years after the injury, so lifelong follow-up is required. A cyclodialysis cleft does the opposite and causes hypotony by opening a suprachoroidal outflow route, though closure of the cleft can produce a sharp pressure spike. Commotio retinae is a self-limited outer retinal disturbance with no bearing on outflow. Lens subluxation can raise pressure by pupillary block or phacomorphic or lens-particle mechanisms, but it is not the recognised high-risk answer for chronic post-traumatic glaucoma.

question: Accommodation needed to view an object 50 cm from the eye:
explanation: , Power:1/focal length in m. 1/0.5=2D A The following transposition is correct: Spherical equivalent of -5.75+6.00@65:

review.explanation: Accommodative demand in dioptres is the reciprocal of the working distance in metres, so 1 divided by 0.5 m equals 2 D. This assumes an emmetropic eye fully corrected for distance and ignores the small difference between the spectacle plane and the eye. The same arithmetic underlies the near add calculation: a 40 cm working distance requires 2.5 D, and a 25 cm distance requires 4 D.
